    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee. Merchants resent the cut that card-issuing banks and payment networks take from every sale, and consumers resent checkout fees for paying by credit card.Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has rightly proposed a rule to end that absurdity.Illinois’ Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, set to take effect in July 2027, bars banks from collecting swipe fees on the sales tax and tip portion of a purchase. But federal law exempts national banks from this kind of state regulation, and Congress extended this protection to state-chartered banks to create parity.Illinois reads that protection as covering only those with a physical branch in the state. A small bank in Iowa serving Illinois customers from across the line may have to comply; an identical institution with an Illinois branch is exempt.>>> The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall StreetThat’s wrong, and the FDIC is right to try to fix it.States have a legitimate, long-standing role in protecting consumers and regulating commerce within their borders. But the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states, and for good reason. Without a strong defense of Commerce Clause principles, a few states can bully the rest into following their rules. For multi-state banks, Congress has already set a reasonable standard.Anyone who has worked on state policy, as I did in Arizona, knows the governing principle: in-state presence. An out-of-state business with a substantial in-state presence—such as a physical location—answers to that state’s rules.When the Supreme Court’s 2018 Wayfair decision let states require remote sellers to collect sales tax, the fight was over whether less than a physical presence could count. Nobody ever suggested opening a store in Arizona would exempt a seller from its sales tax.Illinois’ reading of federal banking law produces exactly that absurd result. The provision at concern, from the Riegle-Neal Act, refers to out-of-state banks’ “branches” in the host state, and Illinois reads that word as a limit. Approve a card purchase for a customer passing through Illinois, with no physical location there, and Illinois may say you are subject to its law. Open a branch, and suddenly you are exempt.The result is a regulatory reach that shrinks as a bank’s presence grows. The few state banks based outside Illinois but with a branch there would be exempt, while the 3,185 state banks the FDIC identifies as potentially affected (most of them small) would not. Those banks could spend the resources to comply, but to get an exemption, they would perversely have to open a branch there.That’s not what Congress set out to do. Riegle-Neal was a law about interstate banking and branching, written when banks served customers through branches and the first iPhone was more than a decade away. When Congress amended it in 1997, the bill’s sponsor was plain about the goal: “The essence of this legislation is to provide parity between state-chartered banks and national banks.”Turning a word that described 1990s banking into a penalty on modern remote service banking gets that purpose backward and destroys parity.>>> The Fed Got It Right; Now Congress Must Do the SameThe FDIC’s proposal applies the sensible reading. Where a host state’s law does not apply to an out-of-state national bank, it does not apply to an out-of-state state bank either, branch or no branch. The rule does not replace state regulation with federal regulation; it restores common sense and legislative intent to a 1990s-era statute.If anything, Illinois’ reading works against state authority. The dual banking system, which lets a bank choose a state or federal charter, is itself an expression of federalism. Make the state charter the costlier one, and, as the FDIC observes, banks could shift to federal charters. That would be a strange victory indeed for states’ rights.It also would be an expensive one. The FDIC estimates the affected state banks would spend about $308 million up front and nearly $7 million a year complying, all to transfer roughly $2.3 million a year in fees from banks to merchants. With 11 other states having explored similar legislation, the problem is unlikely to stay in Illinois.If federal law has gone too far or failed to account for state needs in a card-dependent, network-based economy, it’s Congress’ job to amend it. But no reasonable reading of that framework would exempt a bank for moving into a state while penalizing its competitor for staying home.The FDIC has proposed saying that clearly. It should finalize the rule. A bank shouldn’t have to move into Illinois to get out from under Illinois law.

    Few charges draw complaints from as many directions as the card swipe fee. Merchants resent the cut that card-issuing banks and payment networks take from every sale, and consumers resent checkout fees for paying by credit card.

    Under that pressure, states have begun tiptoeing toward regulating interchange fees, or swipe fees, themselves. The first to act, Illinois, reads federal banking law in a way that lets an out-of-state bank escape its rules only by opening a physical branch there. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has rightly proposed a rule to end that absurdity.

    It has been revealed that illinois’ Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, set to take effect in July 2027, bars banks from collecting swipe fees on the sales tax and tip portion of a purchase. But federal law exempts national banks from this kind of state regulation, and Congress extended this protection to state-chartered banks to create parity.

    In a recent development, illinois reads that protection as covering only those with a physical branch in the state. A small bank in Iowa serving Illinois customers from across the line may have to comply; an identical institution with an Illinois branch is exempt.

    >>> The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall Street.

    That’s wrong, and the FDIC is right to try to fix it.

    Sources indicate that states have a legitimate, long-standing role in protecting consumers and regulating commerce within their borders. But the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate commerce among the states, and for good reason. Without a strong defense of Commerce Clause principles, a few states can bully the rest into following their rules. For multi-state banks, Congress has already set a reasonable standard.

    According to recent reports, anyone who has worked on state policy, as I did in Arizona, knows the governing principle: in-state presence. An out-of-state business with a substantial in-state presence—such as a physical location—answers to that state’s rules.

    According to recent reports, when the Supreme Court’s 2018 Wayfair decision let states require remote sellers to collect sales tax, the fight was over whether less than a physical presence could count. Nobody ever suggested opening a store in Arizona would exempt a seller from its sales tax.

    According to recent reports, illinois’ reading of federal banking law produces exactly that absurd result. The provision at issue, from the Riegle-Neal Act, refers to out-of-state banks’ “branches” in the host state, and Illinois reads that word as a limit. Approve a card purchase for a customer passing through Illinois, with no physical location there, and Illinois may say you are subject to its law. Open a branch, and suddenly you are exempt.

    Recent findings suggest that the result is a regulatory reach that shrinks as a bank’s presence grows. The few state banks based outside Illinois but with a branch there would be exempt, while the 3,185 state banks the FDIC identifies as potentially affected (most of them small) would not. Those banks could spend the resources to comply, but to get an exemption, they would perversely have to open a branch there.

    In a recent development, that’s not what Congress set out to do. Riegle-Neal was a law about interstate banking and branching, written when banks served customers through branches and the first iPhone was more than a decade away. When Congress amended it in 1997, the bill’s sponsor was plain about the goal: “The essence of this legislation is to provide parity between state-chartered banks and national banks.”.

    Turning a word that described 1990s banking into a penalty on modern remote service banking gets that purpose backward and destroys parity.

    >>> The Fed Got It Right; Now Congress Must Do the Same.

    In a recent development, the FDIC’s proposal applies the sensible reading. Where a host state’s law does not apply to an out-of-state national bank, it does not apply to an out-of-state state bank either, branch or no branch. The rule does not replace state regulation with federal regulation; it restores common sense and legislative intent to a 1990s-era statute.

    If anything, Illinois’ reading works against state authority. The dual banking system, which lets a bank choose a state or federal charter, is itself an expression of federalism. Make the state charter the costlier one, and, as the FDIC observes, banks could shift to federal charters. That would be a strange victory indeed for states’ rights.

    It also would be an expensive one. The FDIC estimates the affected state banks would spend about $308 million up front and nearly $7 million a year complying, all to transfer roughly $2.3 million a year in fees from banks to merchants. With 11 other states having explored similar legislation, the problem is unlikely to stay in Illinois.

    Sources indicate that if federal law has gone too far or failed to account for state needs in a card-dependent, network-based economy, it’s Congress’ job to amend it. But no reasonable reading of that framework would exempt a bank for moving into a state while penalizing its competitor for staying home.

    Industry observers note that the FDIC has proposed saying that clearly. It should finalize the rule. A bank shouldn’t have to move into Illinois to get out from under Illinois law.

    Not long ago, I drifted through a handful of old European cities. What stayed with me was neither the cathedrals nor the cafés with their thimbles of ferocious coffee.

    It was the organization the bronze kept: The squares belonged to poets and playwrights, astronomers and philosophers, figures in stone cloaks gazing over bustling pigeons as if weighing one more line. Here and there, a statesman sulked on his plinth, and the courthouses guarded their jurists, but officeholders were scarce.

    The exception was the kings, those equestrian gentlemen forever reining in horses that never move.

    Sources indicate that the pattern has a plausible explanation. Europe was hardly a stranger to electoral politics. Athenian citizens voted in assembly, the Roman Republic chose its consuls, Iceland’s Althing has convened since 930, and Venice elected its doges for roughly 11 centuries.

    So, the scarcity of political monuments cannot be explained by the absence of voting. A better account is that a reputation lasts about as long as the work behind it remains usable.

    >>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State.

    Sources indicate that A literary or scientific achievement keeps functioning. Dante’s “Commedia,” Shakespeare’s plays, and Newton’s “Principia” can still be met directly, without an intermediary, and they answer questions each generation asks anew.

    A statesman’s achievement, by contrast, is tied to the circumstance that called it forth: a treaty, a succession crisis, a levy. Once that circumstance passes, the achievement survives chiefly as historical record. The principal lessons learned from political figures are the consequences of their decisions rather than the reasoning that produced them, which is seldom preserved and less often consulted.

    Political monuments are also unusually exposed to revision. The removal of Lenin statues across the former Eastern Bloc after 1989, and the toppling of Edward Colston in Bristol in 2020, suggest that a statesman’s standing stays open to dispute in a way a poet’s rarely does. Southerners know this quite well, having watched Confederate monuments come down in town after town.

    Sources indicate that which brings me home to Auburn, where the statuary has another temperament altogether. Ours wear shoulder pads. Heisman winners stride eternally outside Jordan-Hare, and Shug Jordan keeps his vigil.

    I love a Saturday on the Plains as dearly as anyone alive. But an athlete’s fame is the briefest bloom in the garden, briefer even than a senator’s. Who toasts the champions of antiquity? The wrestlers and charioteers of Olympia survive mostly because Pindar wrote odes to them. They endure, in other words, by the grace of a poet.

    So it was with a small, private gladness that I read the news: Auburn announced a $22 million investment from the state of Alabama, “championed by Gov. Kay Ivey, an Auburn alumna, to establish the Kay Ivey Institute for Civic Leadership.” At last, we may raise a monument to the kind of figure the Old World remembers.

    Industry observers note that auburn enters a crowded and quickening field. Recently, I mentioned the civics centers popping up across many institutions and states. Ohio has committed $24 million to create civic-education centers at five public universities. The ones to beat are well known: Florida, with its Hamilton School for Classical and Civic Education; Texas, with its School of Civic Leadership and Civitas Institute; and Tennessee, whose Institute of American Civics was established in 2022 by the state’s general assembly.

    In a recent development, these programs now count in the standings too, since City Journal’s fresh college-ranking system rewards institutions that host a School of Civic Thought. It’s high time, isn’t it, that Auburn’s name sat atop that list?

    Recent findings suggest that of our own institute, we know very little. The university notes its academic direction, programming and long-term priorities will be developed in the coming months, so my hopes go out wearing a raincoat.

    >>> A Columbus Day Question—Have We Finally Stopped Distorting Our Past?

    Still, the opportunity is plain. Auburn could gather some of the most distinguished and exacting scholars in the humanities: historians, political theorists, legal minds, and philosophers. Those disciplines are the timbers from which civic life is built.

    According to recent reports, the town’s growing. It’s a fine place to live and think, and its research already commands respect well beyond the state line.

    Industry observers note that the old oaks at Toomer’s Corner stood since the late 1930s. They died because of football. After Auburn beat Alabama in 2010, an aggrieved rival poured herbicide into their roots.

    Their replacements fared little better. One was set ablaze during a celebration after a win over Louisiana State University, and the corner has been replanted more than once since.

    Passion for a game can kill the very things it gathers around. Yet something survived. Saplings grown from the original oaks’ acorns now line the walk from the corner to Samford Hall. The descendants of those trees mark a path from the place where we celebrate to the place where we study.

    According to recent reports, if the Ivey Institute is built with care, more of us may follow that path. Someday, a visitor may find, among the halfbacks, a philosopher in bronze. Better still, he may find generations of graduates who read the founders as eagerly as they read a box score.

    That would be a monument no poison or match could take down.

    In a recent development, the economy exceeded analysts’ expectations in October. Friday’s monthly employment report not only shows an additional 165,000 jobs, but also revises upward the previous two months. Including those revisions, the total increase is just under a quarter million jobs. And the internals of the report are even better.

    According to recent reports, the number of jobs in the report comes from a survey of businesses, but there’s also a survey of households that produces employment and unemployment estimates. This survey indicated that 463,000 more Americans were employed in October than September, and 1.4 million more than July, pushing down the unemployment rate.

    People are entering the labor market in droves, and they’re able to find jobs. That’s why labor force participation has reversed its multi-year slide and is up for three consecutive months, same as the employment-to-population ratio. Americans are not only looking for jobs but finding them.

    There’s even good news on the types of jobs being created. All net job growth last month came from full-time work, while part-time jobs actually declined as people moved from part-time to full-time work. Additionally, the number of people with multiple jobs declined, signally many folks exchanged multiple part-time jobs for a single full-time one. Another sign of labor market strength.

    >>> Americans, Job Market Need Workforce Pell Grants.

    Since July, full-time jobs are now up a whopping 1.5 million while part-time jobs have declined, so all net job growth over the last three months has been full-time work, which tends to have better pay and benefits compared to part-time.

    There’s more good news regarding where all these jobs are being created. More than 96 percent of October’s job growth came from the productive private sector. The government added only 6,000 jobs, all of which came from state governments while the federal bureaucracy added no jobs at all.

    Recent findings suggest that within the private sector, most areas of the economy added jobs in October, including manufacturing. This sector in particular is noteworthy because payrolls were declining for three years as the sector hemorrhaged jobs from 2023 through 2025. That downward trend was finally reversed this year, and now manufacturing jobs are at their highest level since December 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that so, despite all the fearmongering of AI taking everyone’s job, employers went on a hiring spree last month and Americans are pouring into the labor market. This dynamic was especially true of college graduates, a group that was supposed to be directly in the crosshairs of AI, but whose employment level shot up by 422,000 in October.

    Industry observers note that that means the number of college grads working today is more than 2 million higher than in July. To be clear, AI is certainly eliminating some jobs, and that will continue as the technology evolves and is adopted. But it’s also creating even more opportunities for work, just like any disruptive technology, from the steam locomotive to the internet.

    >>> Why Aren’t Employers Hiring Right Now?

    It should be no surprise that when student loan repayment restarted, millions of college grads decided to look for work again. Having a bill to pay—instead of foisting that debt on the backs of taxpayers—is a powerful motivator to find work, even if you have a gender studies degree.

    Industry observers note that ending the student loan repayment “pauses” that began six years ago is just one example of how current public policy is promoting a strong labor market. Throw in tax cuts like full expensing for businesses along with massive reductions in burdensome regulations and you have a great landscape to increase economic growth and employment.

    Tax and regulatory reform are principally responsible for the economy being on track to increase private fixed investment by 10 percent or more this year. That category of investment is extremely important because it’s the driver of long-run economic growth. It’s where we get everything from factories to software—all the things that increase productivity and wage growth.

    That increased wage growth is already here, but it’s been swallowed by higher energy prices ever since February due to the Iran war. Although the average American’s weekly paycheck bought less in October than it did in February, it’s at least estimated to have bought slightly more than in September.

    Industry observers note that the fallout from the Iran war is the only fly in the ointment from the October jobs report. Were it not for higher prices, workers would grade this economy an “A plus.”.

    Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

    Recent findings suggest that after a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

    Recent findings suggest that market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

    It has been revealed that democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to fresh data centers had been building.

    Recent findings suggest that investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

    >>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

    It has been revealed that the fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

    It has been revealed that the fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

    Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer new commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

    Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

    Those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

    >>> Slowing Data Center Construction Signals the Need for Pro-Growth Reforms.

    Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

    So the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either. And while the tax-reform legislation passed last year obviously did require Congress, most of its provisions are permanent and won’t need reauthorization.

    Recent findings suggest that the administration retains broad authority to glitch executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

    Democrats will certainly try to slow that good work. Their leaders are already planning a wave of made-for-cable show trials that will drain time and attention from officials who should be dismantling the bureaucracy. But investigations can only delay regulatory reform, not stop it.

    It has been revealed that the president’s veto is another silver lining that will likely prevent the Democratic Congress from enacting sweeping tax hikes or newly introduced regulatory regimes. The worst ideas will hopefully die in committee or an Oval Office waste basket.

    Sources indicate that the economy has weathered worse than a hostile Congress. Ongoing deregulation and existing tax reform are still tailwinds for economic growth while the veto pen is there to stop headwinds as they arise. The outlook might be blue, but it’s not black and blue.

By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.>>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”The Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.The combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.The damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile releases, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each.     Last December, President Donald Trump introduced his vision for the United States Navy: a 30-year shipbuilding proposal called the “Golden Fleet.” Flanking him during his unveiling of this plan were renderings of a core component of that future Navy: USS Defiant, the lead ship of a latest, modern class of battleship. But delivering it faces significant hurdles. The first is realistically addressing the Navy’s shaky shipbuilding track record. The second is surviving the changed political reality in Washington—made more challenging by Trump’s original plan to name the class of warship after himself.

    By any name, the battleship addresses critical needs for the U.S. Navy. A modern battleship’s firepower, command and control, and data-fusion capabilities have been proven vital in recent conflicts in the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Persian Gulf. Mitigating shipbuilding risks, such as constrained production capacity and the integration of numerous advanced technologies, necessitate a continuous testing regimen that scales up as the ships are built.

    Industry observers note that the U.S. Navy Could Use a Modern “Battlecruiser” Warship.

    Industry observers note that the unveiling of the battleship comes as the Navy faces the imminent loss of significant at-sea firepower. By 2031, the departures of various submarines, cruisers, and destroyers will see nearly 2,000 missile-launch tubes lost. To blunt this loss, the next iteration of Virginia-class nuclear submarines will carry 28 hypersonic missiles, and the Navy’s unmanned vessels may also begin to carry offensive weapons.

    >>> The U.S. Navy Must Build the “Golden Fleet”.

    Industry observers note that the Navy missed an opportunity to address this firepower dilemma with its aborted CG(X) next-generation cruiser program, abandoned in 2011. These forced aging destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers to continue shouldering the air and missile defense responsibilities for carrier strike groups. Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, however, lack the firepower and crew to fully assume the cruiser mission. The Arleigh Burke-class has 96 missile tubes, against 122 on the Ticonderoga-class, and has limited berthing for the needed staff to manage air and missile defenses for the carrier strike group.

    In the long term, the Defiant and subsequent battleships are intended to fill this mission and firepower gap. The Defiant, with its added firepower, sensors and crew, will take over the Ticonderoga-class warships’ responsibilities for defending carrier strike groups. The ship will also employ long-range hypersonic missiles in support of carrier air-strike operations to rapidly suppress emerging threats.

    It has been revealed that the combination of capabilities merged in Defiant with sustained high speeds makes the vessel more closely resemble a battlecruiser—a high-speed battleship able to deliver long-range firepower and defend the carrier strike group from air and missile threats. However, recent battle lessons are creating another critical mission.

    According to recent reports, the damage inflicted upon U.S. Fifth Fleet Headquarters in Bahrain, and its temporary evacuation due to Iranian missile debuts, demonstrates the vulnerability of permanent land-based naval installations to air attack. Moving headquarters to sea is one way to mitigate this danger, and follows a long tradition of numbered fleet command ships. A battlecruiser with robust command and control capabilities can maintain a common operational picture with the warships and unmanned platforms of its numbered fleet, reducing the Navy’s reliance on global communications.

    >>> To Build the Golden Fleet.

    How the Defiant Can Clear the Political Minefield on Capitol Hill.

    While battlecruisers are needed now, the United States faces numerous constraints that must be navigated before they can join the Golden Fleet. The high build cost of these ships will likely stir substantial resistance from budget-conscious members of Congress; a bill estimated by the Congressional Budget Office to be upwards of $23 billion for the first and subsequent ships costing $18 billion each. There are also serious shortages of skilled workers capable of efficiently building such intricate and substantial ships. Moreover, establishing newly introduced or expanding existing shipyards to build these battlecruisers requires working through onerous shipbuilding regulations.

    According to recent reports, keeping Congress’ support will necessitate reducing the potential for cost overruns and program delays. One way to accomplish this is to use proven technologies and systems in the initial design. Doing this would result in Defiant embracing existing systems to meet its mission requirements the soonest. Integrating systems like the hypersonic missile technologies being developed for the Zumwalt-class destroyers and the new AN/SPY-6 radars being installed in Arleigh Burke-class vessels will further compress production timelines.

    In time, the design will need to be improved on through continuous updates—one being the transition to nuclear power to sustain high speeds and pace the aircraft carrier the battlecruiser is intended to protect. One option is using the same A1B nuclear power plant now used in the Ford-class aircraft carriers, given enough time for production to ramp up to support aircraft carrier and battlecruiser production.

    It has been revealed that resurrecting the battlecruiser for modern naval missions is a highly ambitious strategy, and it may yet fall through. But it is needed to equip the U.S. Navy with the capabilities for fighting a modern naval war across the Pacific.

    This piece originally appeared in The National Interest.

    Latest Update: Rule 14a-8: Perhaps Slow-Walking Recission is Best

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission.
    • In a recent development, in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission.
    • To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, in a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the issue, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having noted that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.For example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.The current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.While our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”>>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation ProposalsTo illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a organization would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.Third, sustainability commitments are said to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.Finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.If these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford. Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.>>> More Than Ever, It’s Time for Economic Freedom, Not DEI or ESGAll the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.Yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.All the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too swiftly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.Much more can, should, and will be said about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. But for now, it is worth noting that a consistent theme animates Heritage’s past and present positions on Rule 14a-8. Heritage certainly appreciates the ways we are witnessing private ordering, federalism, and the marketplace of ideas operating in response to the proposed rescission of the rule, but we are in fact happy “with the SEC’s direction of travel.”.

    Please enjoy the latest edition of Short Circuit, a weekly feature written by a bunch of people at the Institute for Justice.

    Victory! Millions of Americans want and need low-FODMAP foods, which are low in certain sugars that can cause debilitating stomach complications, aggravate irritable bowels, and worse. Fortunately, this week (following the Ninth Circuit's revival of our First Amendment challenge), the FDA lifted its ban on producers truthfully labelling their products "Low-FODMAP." Says IJ client Michelle Przybocki, who abides by a strict low-FODMAP diet after nearly dying from digestive complications, "I'm thrilled that the federal government is going to allow companies to start labeling their products as 'Low-FODMAP,' because this makes it easier for me to find foods that I know will not cause me digestive issues." Click here to learn more.

    New on the Short Circuit podcast: Fancy some Elevenses? Serving up Eleventh Circuit refreshments in our #12Months12Circuits series. There's excessive bail in Alabama and excessive bar fees in Florida.

    It has been revealed that friends, if a federal official violates your constitutional rights, your options for being made whole by money damages have been all but extinguished in recent years, leaving the feds with something akin to absolute immunity for all kinds of misconduct and misdeeds. But there has to be some avenue for accountability. So here at IJ, we're pushing back, not only on the late-lamented Bivens cause of action, but also on the too-narrowly construed Federal Tort Claims Act. And then, of course, there's the traditional source of accountability that the Founders would have recognized (and that the Supreme Court's Bivens skeptics preferred): state law causes of action, like California's traditional tort system and the state's Bane Act. All of which were on the table at oral argument in the Ninth Circuit this week, where we're happy to report we had an engaged, cross-ideological panel. Click here to learn more.

    • Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s new theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations.

He held that conflict is neither imminent nor inevitable. This status quo, he said, can be sustained by clearly articulating NATO’s intentions, maintaining open lines of communication with external states, and maintaining deterrence by denial through military capacity.Commenting on the character of NATO, General Grynkewich stressed that the Alliance is defensive and has “no intends, no intentions, and no ambitions” other than the protection of NATO peoples and territories. SACEUR nevertheless cautioned potential adversaries not to mistake NATO’s defensive nature for a lack of resolve and emphasized that member states will ensure any attack on Alliance territory will prove futile.[REF]This point was underlined by additional commentary regarding NATO’s deterrence posture. General Grynkewich drew attention to the Alliance’s “decision advantage.” He asserted that NATO will not be caught by surprise thanks to an immense intelligence footprint encompassing a vast network of sensors and sources. General Grynkewich framed NATO’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capability as a key enabler of the Alliance’s theory of victory. By rapidly assessing an opposing force’s presence and intent, NATO forces will have time to mobilize in the numbers required to deny attackers at the point of contact, especially because these troops will be reinforcing significant numbers of NATO troops forward positioned within NATO’s easternmost states.Because of NATO’s doctrine, character, and posture, General Grynkewich remarked that the burden of escalation will always lie upon NATO’s aggressors. NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy seeks only to prevent an enemy from realizing its revisionist aspirations. He plainly asserted that such states will “bear the full moral, political, and strategic weight” of initiating and expanding conflict with the Alliance.[REF]General Grynkewich included within this posture of deterrence and denial an explicit characterization of NATO’s intentions after the outbreak of conflict. He emphasized that the Alliance’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy does not seek at the outset to impose a strategic defeat upon its adversaries. Instead, NATO seeks simply to employ its theory of victory to maintain the Alliance’s territorial integrity by tactically defeating its attackers.In sum, General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to communicate fundamental Alliance convictions to audiences both within and outside NATO. He articulated how NATO is not simply relying on decades-old defense strategies but adopting new means to meet emerging security threats. He delineated an internal Alliance dynamic defined by cohesion anchored in a collective determination to defend Alliance territory from opportunistic adversaries. He portrayed to external audiences a NATO whose mandate is limited to protecting its citizens and territory but that is also unified and firm in its willingness to fight and to defeat an aggressor if needed. General Grynkewich confidently messaged to Russia that he wants to assure those who “might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”[REF]Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation.

    On October 12, 2026, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s new theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations. General Grynkewich’s deterrence-focused theory of victory struck the right tone, reassuring worried allies and signaling to Moscow that the United States and its NATO allies are confident of their ability to defeat a Russian incursion into a NATO state and that Russia would do well not to consider one. The speech and the strategy itself also appear wisely designed to avoid unnecessary escalation with Russia as SACEUR made clear throughout that NATO is a defensive Alliance.

If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”[REF].

    Sources indicate that during the Cold War, West Germany was the NATO state considered most likely to be attacked by massive numbers of Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, and the Fulda Gap was often identified as the most likely attack route. The geographic size of West Germany meant that NATO forces could fall back tens or hundreds of kilometers before they could generate enough combat mass to begin a counteroffensive against Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces and then expel them from NATO soil. In this sense, NATO planned to trade territory for time, during which it would seize the conventional advantage.

    Today, the Suwalki Gap between Lithuania and Poland is often cited as the modern equivalent of the Fulda Gap, especially because it separates Russian-allied Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.[REF] The three Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are for numerous reasons the NATO states against which full-scale Russian aggression is most likely; for example, Russian revanchists claim the existence of Russian-speaking minorities in Estonia and Latvia as a potential pretext, and Russian military planners could seek to connect the Russian exclave by land to either Belarus or Russia, and Lithuania is in their way. In the Baltic States, Block, Blunt, Break makes sense as the strategy for deterring or defending against Russian aggression from both a military planning and a political perspective.

    From a military planning perspective, the lack of strategic depth in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania was likely a major factor in the change in strategy. Blocking the Russian advance from the outset prevents the Russians from gaining a foothold that may prove difficult to dislodge once fortified and reinforced.

Should Russia rapidly gain lodgment within Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, it could then sue for peace before NATO could dislodge Russian forces and liberate those three NATO members. This could well create real political divisions within the North Atlantic Council, in which some countries would press for the liberation of the Baltic States, while others may seek to accept the peace proposal. It is not inconceivable that such a development could lead to the fracturing and potential breakup of NATO—long a goal of Moscow. This fresh strategy articulated by SACEUR could be a way to defend every inch of NATO soil from the outset and prevent this difficult scenario.

    Does Board and Management Diversity Improve Financial Performance? The Evidence Is Weak

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3426 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Heritage

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history.
    • In 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history.
    • Especially in the wake of a fresh report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history. Huff’s central insight—that correlation dressed in the vestments of causation can seduce even careful readers—has aged better than most mid-century paperbacks. It’s due for a revival.Especially in the wake of a newly introduced report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.The report is not without ambition. It draws on federal EEO-1 workforce filings matched to financial data for 1,482 publicly traded companies between 2016 and 2024, and it contains some genuine quantitative analysis.But its empirical research design is deeply flawed, and in ways Huff would have recognized instantly. The analysis may document correlations inside a selected dataset, but it does not establish that management diversity improves corporate performance, that DEI programs create shareholder value, or that companies incur financial risk by scaling those programs back.Consider, first, the sample, always the place a skeptical reader should look, and always the place such reports hope one will not. The number of observed companies changes substantially by year, reaching 1,059 workforce observations in 2020 and falling to 523 in 2024. Earlier data combine voluntary disclosures with records obtained through a Department of Labor Freedom of Information Act release. Later data rely heavily on voluntary disclosure alone, a shift roughly analogous to switching, mid-poll, from a mandatory census to a call for volunteers.>>> DEI’s Days in the Corporate World Are NumberedThe report itself concedes the consequence: companies choosing to disclose had 4.5 percentage points more BIPOC management representation than companies that never disclosed. Selection into the sample is therefore entangled with the very variable under study, which is a polite way of saying the study measures, in part, itself.Nor does the report tell readers how its companies compare with the Russell 3000 or the CRSP-Compustat universe, the benchmarks against which any claim to represent “corporate America” must be tested. Readers do not learn whether the sample differs in size, industry, age, profitability, exchange listing, geographic exposure, or prior stock performance.These are not incidental details; they are precisely the characteristics that predict both workforce composition and financial outcomes. Pooling a large technology company with a small regional manufacturer and regressing profits on a single demographic measure does not make those differences disappear. It merely makes them invisible.The changing sample, moreover, weakens whatever trends the report reports. An average can move for two quite different reasons: because the same firms changed, or because different firms wandered into and out of the dataset. To its credit, the report acknowledges that sample composition may explain part of the sharp decline in female representation it reports for financial services between 2020 and 2021.That caveat, once granted, applies throughout the time series, a fact the report is less eager to grant. A balanced panel and a decomposition of within-firm change from sample entry and exit are prerequisites, not refinements, for interpreting these averages as corporate trends rather than statistical artifacts of who happened to show up.Measurement supplies a second problem, and a subtler one. EEO-1 filings are more standardized than ordinary ESG ratings, which is a modest compliment, but they still require decisions about establishments, corporate ownership, mergers, missing filings, and the aggregation of executive, senior, first-line, and mid-level managers. The report provides too little information to reproduce those choices. Its Racial Justice Initiative score is even less transparent. It combines 27 indicators—ranging from promotion data and EEO-1 disclosure to public statements, donations, and references to political movements—with some categories assigned five times the weight of others. One is invited to trust the recipe without seeing the kitchen.The ESG measurement literature explains, with some precision, why these choices matter. Florian Berg, Julian Kölbel, and Roberto Rigobon compared six major ESG rating systems and found correlations ranging from 0.38 to 0.71, hardly the tight clustering one would expect if these systems were measuring the same underlying reality. They attribute 56% of rating divergence to measurement, 38% to scope, and 6% to weighting.Any claimed DEI-performance relationship therefore raises a prior question, one the report never quite gets around to asking: What DEI score is being used, which indicators enter it, and how are they weighted? A composite social score cannot be treated as an objective corporate trait without its coding rules, missing-data procedures, reliability checks, and sensitivity to alternative weights. Put simply, DEI and ESG scores vary so markedly across providers that they have largely lost their meaning as fixed facts about a company.Related research by Christos Makridis and Majeed Simaan demonstrates that this measurement noise is not merely an academic nuisance; it has real consequences for actual investment decisions. Using more than 22,000 firm-year observations and 21 years of out-of-sample portfolio tests, they find that portfolios incorporating Refinitiv ESG scores do not consistently outperform return-based strategies on a risk-adjusted basis. ESG-only rules can produce higher average returns in some specifications, true enough, but they also generate greater volatility and downside risk (the fine print investors are seldom shown).Return-based factor models achieve comparable or better ex-post ESG standing without using ESG ratings directly at all. Their panel analysis also finds that market volatility predicts later ESG ratings, while ESG ratings do not predict later volatility, suggesting the ratings absorb information the market already knew rather than furnishing anything so useful as foresight.Capturing the Diversity Benefit then commits its largest error, and here Huff would surely have reached for his red pen: it estimates simple bivariate regressions. Financial performance depends on firm size, book-to-market ratios, profitability, investment, leverage, industry, firm age, prior performance, and macroeconomic conditions. The main analysis controls for none of them. This omission is especially damaging because the report’s own tables show sharply different results across market-capitalization groups. The authors call firm size “almost certainly” a confound—then proceed, undeterred, to present unadjusted aggregate estimates anyway.Income after tax, measured in dollars, illustrates the difficulty. Large companies generally earn more dollars and may also employ more diverse managers. A positive coefficient can therefore capture company scale rather than operating performance—correlation masquerading, once again, as insight.Raw multiyear stock-price appreciation is similarly inadequate to the task. Finance researchers evaluate abnormal returns only after accounting for established sources of risk and return. The Fama-French five-factor model incorporates market exposure, size, value, profitability, and investment; cross-sectional work commonly employs the Fama-MacBeth method to test whether a given characteristic predicts returns after competing explanations have had their say. The report employs none of this.Timing presents yet another serious obstacle. Matching workforce composition in a given year with performance measured in that same year does not reveal which came first. Strong companies may simply have more resources to recruit broadly, invest in management systems, and publish workforce data in the first place. Both diversity and performance may reflect nothing more exotic than management quality itself. Showing that a correlation existed before 2020 does not resolve the question of reverse causality. It merely pushes it back a few years. At a minimum, the analysis should use lagged representation to predict future outcomes, control for prior performance, and account for the swath of unobserved differences across firms over time.The report also runs hundreds of statistical tests across demographic groups—approximately 15 outcomes, 11 sectors, three size categories, and nine years. At a 5% significance threshold, false positives become not merely possible but inevitable when researchers search across that many combinations. It would be more surprising if nothing turned up significant by chance alone. Yet the tables display only plus signs, minus signs, and blanks. They omit coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and economic magnitudes—the very information a reader would need to judge whether “significant” means “large” or merely “detectable.” The analysis should identify a small set of primary outcomes and adjust for multiple testing accordingly.Prior research illustrates why this quantitative discipline matters so greatly. Jeremiah Green and John Hand attempted to reproduce McKinsey’s influential diversity-performance findings using observable S&P 500 data and found no statistically reliable relationship between executive racial and ethnic diversity and industry-adjusted profitability, sales growth, return on assets, return on equity, or total shareholder return. Their critique also identifies reverse causality in relating later diversity measures to earlier performance—the chicken-and-egg problem dressed in academic clothing.>>> The Myth of “Voluntary” ESGAlex Edmans, Caroline Flammer, and Simon Glossner draw an equally notable conceptual distinction. Their employee-survey measure of DEI has little correlation with demographic representation as such. It is associated with stronger future accounting performance, earnings surprises, and valuation ratios while demographic diversity, on its own, is not. The DEI measure also does not predict future stock returns. Representation, inclusion, and corporate programs are, in short, different constructs measuring different things, and the report moves among them with a freedom the evidence does not license.Which raises the damning question: if DEI scores do not reliably reflect a company’s actual demographic composition, doesn’t the entire argument collapse under its own premise?None of this forecloses the possibility that a serious analysis might yet find that management diversity contains financially relevant information. The current report has simply not demonstrated it. The authors should compare their sample with the public-company universe, publish their data construction and coding rules, use a balanced panel, estimate models with firm and year fixed effects, control for standard company characteristics, evaluate factor-adjusted returns, lag the workforce variables, and correct for multiple testing. They should also report effect sizes rather than colored symbols, which are decorative rather than dispositive.Until then, the defensible conclusion is a modest one: among the company-years observed in this selectively disclosed dataset, some measures of management representation correlate with some financial outcomes. That could well be the case. But it does not establish a “diversity benefit,” and the distance between those two claims is the whole of the matter. Corporate leaders should demand better evidence before accepting a financial claim simply because it supports a preferred social or political conclusion. The same standard, it hardly needs saying, should apply when the conclusion cuts in the opposite direction. Huff, one suspects, would have appreciated the symmetry.

    Industry observers note that the report is not without ambition. It draws on federal EEO-1 workforce filings matched to financial data for 1,482 publicly traded companies between 2016 and 2024, and it contains some genuine quantitative analysis.

    Sources indicate that but its empirical research design is deeply flawed, and in ways Huff would have recognized instantly. The analysis may document correlations inside a selected dataset, but it does not establish that management diversity improves corporate performance, that DEI programs create shareholder value, or that companies incur financial risk by scaling those programs back.

    According to recent reports, consider, first, the sample, always the place a skeptical reader should look, and always the place such reports hope one will not. The number of observed companies changes substantially by year, reaching 1,059 workforce observations in 2020 and falling to 523 in 2024. Earlier data combine voluntary disclosures with records obtained through a Department of Labor Freedom of Information Act release. Later data rely heavily on voluntary disclosure alone, a shift roughly analogous to switching, mid-poll, from a mandatory census to a call for volunteers.

    >>> DEI’s Days in the Corporate World Are Numbered.

    The report itself concedes the consequence: companies choosing to disclose had 4.5 percentage points more BIPOC management representation than companies that never disclosed. Selection into the sample is therefore entangled with the very variable under study, which is a polite way of saying the study measures, in part, itself.

    Industry observers note that nor does the report tell readers how its companies compare with the Russell 3000 or the CRSP-Compustat universe, the benchmarks against which any claim to represent “corporate America” must be tested. Readers do not learn whether the sample differs in size, industry, age, profitability, exchange listing, geographic exposure, or prior stock performance.

    These are not incidental details; they are precisely the characteristics that predict both workforce composition and financial outcomes. Pooling a large technology company with a small regional manufacturer and regressing profits on a single demographic measure does not make those differences disappear. It merely makes them invisible.

    The changing sample, moreover, weakens whatever trends the report reports. An average can move for two quite different reasons: because the same firms changed, or because different firms wandered into and out of the dataset. To its credit, the report acknowledges that sample composition may explain part of the sharp decline in female representation it reports for financial services between 2020 and 2021.

    That caveat, once granted, applies throughout the time series, a fact the report is less eager to grant. A balanced panel and a decomposition of within-firm change from sample entry and exit are prerequisites, not refinements, for interpreting these averages as corporate trends rather than statistical artifacts of who happened to show up.

    Recent findings suggest that measurement supplies a second problem, and a subtler one. EEO-1 filings are more standardized than ordinary ESG ratings, which is a modest compliment, but they still require decisions about establishments, corporate ownership, mergers, missing filings, and the aggregation of executive, senior, first-line, and mid-level managers. The report provides too little information to reproduce those choices. Its Racial Justice Initiative score is even less transparent. It combines 27 indicators—ranging from promotion data and EEO-1 disclosure to public statements, donations, and references to political movements—with some categories assigned five times the weight of others. One is invited to trust the recipe without seeing the kitchen.

    The ESG measurement literature explains, with some precision, why these choices matter. Florian Berg, Julian Kölbel, and Roberto Rigobon compared six major ESG rating systems and found correlations ranging from 0.38 to 0.71, hardly the tight clustering one would expect if these systems were measuring the same underlying reality. They attribute 56% of rating divergence to measurement, 38% to scope, and 6% to weighting.

    It has been revealed that any claimed DEI-performance relationship therefore raises a prior question, one the report never quite gets around to asking: What DEI score is being used, which indicators enter it, and how are they weighted? A composite social score cannot be treated as an objective corporate trait without its coding rules, missing-data procedures, reliability checks, and sensitivity to alternative weights. Put simply, DEI and ESG scores vary so markedly across providers that they have largely lost their meaning as fixed facts about a manufacturer.

    Related research by Christos Makridis and Majeed Simaan demonstrates that this measurement noise is not merely an academic nuisance; it has real consequences for actual investment decisions. Using more than 22,000 firm-year observations and 21 years of out-of-sample portfolio tests, they find that portfolios incorporating Refinitiv ESG scores do not consistently outperform return-based strategies on a risk-adjusted basis. ESG-only rules can produce higher average returns in some specifications, true enough, but they also generate greater volatility and downside risk (the fine print investors are seldom shown).

    Sources indicate that return-based factor models achieve comparable or better ex-post ESG standing without using ESG ratings directly at all. Their panel analysis also finds that market volatility predicts later ESG ratings, while ESG ratings do not predict later volatility, suggesting the ratings absorb information the market already knew rather than furnishing anything so useful as foresight.

    Capturing the Diversity Benefit then commits its largest error, and here Huff would surely have reached for his red pen: it estimates simple bivariate regressions. Financial performance depends on firm size, book-to-market ratios, profitability, investment, leverage, industry, firm age, prior performance, and macroeconomic conditions. The main analysis controls for none of them. This omission is especially damaging because the report’s own tables show sharply different results across market-capitalization groups. The authors call firm size “almost certainly” a confound—then proceed, undeterred, to present unadjusted aggregate estimates anyway.

    Recent findings suggest that income after tax, measured in dollars, illustrates the difficulty. Large companies generally earn more dollars and may also employ more diverse managers. A positive coefficient can therefore capture company scale rather than operating performance—correlation masquerading, once again, as insight.

    Raw multiyear stock-price appreciation is similarly inadequate to the task. Finance researchers evaluate abnormal returns only after accounting for established sources of risk and return. The Fama-French five-factor model incorporates market exposure, size, value, profitability, and investment; cross-sectional work commonly employs the Fama-MacBeth method to test whether a given characteristic predicts returns after competing explanations have had their say. The report employs none of this.

    Sources indicate that timing presents yet another serious obstacle. Matching workforce composition in a given year with performance measured in that same year does not reveal which came first. Strong companies may simply have more resources to recruit broadly, invest in management systems, and publish workforce data in the first place. Both diversity and performance may reflect nothing more exotic than management quality itself. Showing that a correlation existed before 2020 does not resolve the question of reverse causality. It merely pushes it back a few years. At a minimum, the analysis should use lagged representation to predict future outcomes, control for prior performance, and account for the swath of unobserved differences across firms over time.

    It has been revealed that the report also runs hundreds of statistical tests across demographic groups—approximately 15 outcomes, 11 sectors, three size categories, and nine years. At a 5% significance threshold, false positives become not merely possible but inevitable when researchers search across that many combinations. It would be more surprising if nothing turned up significant by chance alone. Yet the tables display only plus signs, minus signs, and blanks. They omit coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and economic magnitudes—the very information a reader would need to judge whether “significant” means “large” or merely “detectable.” The analysis should identify a small set of primary outcomes and adjust for multiple testing accordingly.

    Prior research illustrates why this quantitative discipline matters so greatly. Jeremiah Green and John Hand attempted to reproduce McKinsey’s influential diversity-performance findings using observable S&P 500 data and found no statistically reliable relationship between executive racial and ethnic diversity and industry-adjusted profitability, sales growth, return on assets, return on equity, or total shareholder return. Their critique also identifies reverse causality in relating later diversity measures to earlier performance—the chicken-and-egg problem dressed in academic clothing.

    >>> The Myth of “Voluntary” ESG.

    Alex Edmans, Caroline Flammer, and Simon Glossner draw an equally important conceptual distinction. Their employee-survey measure of DEI has little correlation with demographic representation as such. It is associated with stronger future accounting performance, earnings surprises, and valuation ratios while demographic diversity, on its own, is not. The DEI measure also does not predict future stock returns. Representation, inclusion, and corporate programs are, in short, different constructs measuring different things, and the report moves among them with a freedom the evidence does not license.

    Which raises the damning question: if DEI scores do not reliably reflect a firm’s actual demographic composition, doesn’t the entire argument collapse under its own premise?

    Industry observers note that none of this forecloses the possibility that a serious analysis might yet find that management diversity contains financially relevant information. The current report has simply not demonstrated it. The authors should compare their sample with the public-organization universe, publish their data construction and coding rules, use a balanced panel, estimate models with firm and year fixed effects, control for standard company characteristics, evaluate factor-adjusted returns, lag the workforce variables, and correct for multiple testing. They should also report effect sizes rather than colored symbols, which are decorative rather than dispositive.

    Until then, the defensible conclusion is a modest one: among the company-years observed in this selectively disclosed dataset, some measures of management representation correlate with some financial outcomes. That could well be the case. But it does not establish a “diversity benefit,” and the distance between those two claims is the whole of the matter. Corporate leaders should demand better evidence before accepting a financial claim simply because it supports a preferred social or political conclusion. The same standard, it hardly needs saying, should apply when the conclusion cuts in the opposite direction. Huff, one suspects, would have appreciated the symmetry.

    💡 Key Takeaways
