    • In a recent development, critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the upcoming agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that introductionPresident Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.Critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the newly introduced agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF]The new agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.U.S. Strategic InterestThe agreement details the core U.S. national security interests at stake and the rationale behind the push for an expanded agreement, “[r]ecognizing the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and “[n]oting that the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”[REF]The strategic rationale for American interest in securing Greenland from adversarial influence and maintaining a military presence is enduring, rational, and grounded in more than a century of U.S. strategic thinking.[REF] It is strongest when considered in the context of great-power competition and homeland defense, as the Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) heading toward the U.S. and Greenland in particular lies on the shortest and most likely path for these systems when they are fired from Russia.[REF] During the Cold War, both the United States and the Soviet Union operated submarines under the polar ice cap, tested weapons, and invested heavily in surveillance and early warning systems across the land, air, sea, and undersea domains because of the same geographic and strategic realities.Greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland–Iceland–U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass.[REF] It is notable for the United States and its NATO allies to maintain awareness of Russian and Chinese submarines passing through this area, especially ballistic missile submarines equipped with nuclear weapons.The airspace above Greenland is also critically important to defending the U.S. homeland, as U.S. military radars in Greenland contribute to the detection of any hostile ballistic missile movements toward North America.[REF] Because the Arctic is the shortest path between Russia and the United States and between China and the United States, Russian ICBMs, strategic bombers, and hypersonic and cruise missiles would most likely traverse the Arctic on course for the U.S. in the event of a war—a fact that led Washington to negotiate the 1951 Defense Agreement with Denmark early in the Cold War. North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), a binational U.S.–Canada command, requires persistent Arctic and High North domain awareness to fulfill its core mission of defending the continent’s airspace.[REF] During the Cold War, the U.S. had an extended network of manned radar installations across the Arctic known as the Distant Early Warning Line (DEW Line), but it closed much of this network during the 1990s after the Cold War ended.[REF] The U.S. also operated a series of air and naval bases across Greenland that were likewise closed during the 1990s.Today, with the return of great-power competition with China and Russia, Washington has recognized the need to rebuild this Arctic infrastructure as an essential element of continental defense. Pituffik Space Base in Greenland is one of the central nodes in this architecture because its Upgraded Early Warning Radar is one of only a few U.S. or allied sensors providing ballistic missile warning and space surveillance coverage of the North Atlantic and polar approaches to North America.The United States is increasing its engagement in the Arctic region in several ways, and the increased U.S. activity in Greenland is closely interconnected with other major national security projects being undertaken by the Trump Administration. For example, in view of the long-standing U.S. icebreaker shortage, Pituffik Space Base at the moment relies on a Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker for its annual resupply, given the longtime U.S. icebreaker shortage.[REF] The Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, or ICE Pact, seeks to remedy this shortage by building a much larger U.S. fleet of icebreakers in collaboration with Finland and Canada.[REF] The Trump Administration’s Golden Dome initiative to defend the North American continent from missile threats likewise has a major Arctic component and is mentioned in the Greenland agreement’s preamble as one of the shared interests of the three parties.[REF]Danish and Greenlandic InterestGreenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It enjoys a significant degree of self-rule, but responsibility for defense and foreign policy remains primarily with the Danish government in Copenhagen.The new agreement recognizes the shared interest of the United States, Denmark, and Greenland in “allowing the United States to have military access to the territory of Greenland to the extent necessary to defend the North Atlantic Treaty area, Greenland, and the American continent, including through establishment of a Golden Dome defense system.”[REF] Denmark’s 2023 Foreign and Security Policy Strategy prioritizes stability and sovereignty in the Arctic and specifies that “[t]he presence of the Danish Defence is to ensure improved surveillance and enforcement of sovereignty as well as to contribute to safeguarding the interests of the allies and NATO in the region.”[REF]China has demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region. Chinese investments, for example, have targeted Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.[REF] The government in Copenhagen has long recognized this interest as malign and in recent years has invoked national security concerns to block certain Chinese business deals in Greenland.[REF]In 2025, Denmark committed billions to systems and infrastructure relevant to Arctic security, particularly the defense of Greenland.[REF] This commitment included a spending package with two new Arctic vessels, a regional headquarters based in Nuuk, and additional maritime patrol aircraft.[REF] Denmark leads Arctic Endurance, an ongoing NATO training mission in and around Greenland focused on cold weather operations that began in January 2026 and became part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry a month later.[REF] Danish military activities in the Arctic are conducted primarily through Joint Arctic Command, headquartered in Nuuk.[REF]Denmark has long been a reliable and capable U.S. ally and member of NATO. Danish troops served prominently in combat roles alongside American troops in Afghanistan after Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty was invoked in response to the September 11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates among NATO allies.[REF] Denmark spent 3.2 percent of gross domestic product on defense as of 2025—one of the highest percentages in the NATO alliance—and is projected to be among the first NATO allies to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the very near future.[REF] Much of Denmark’s new spending will be to procure high-end capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory in Greenland.[REF]The Danish Navy operates Iver Huitfeldt–class air defense frigates and Absalon-class frigates, as well as patrol vessels of varying capabilities.[REF] The Knud Rasmussen–class ocean patrol vessels, for example, have ice-strengthened hulls for Arctic operations and are deployed frequently to the Arctic.[REF] In 2026, Denmark confirmed a shipbuilding strategy that included the production of five new Arctic ships for the Danish Navy.[REF] This increased naval capacity will reinforce enhanced NATO maritime domain awareness and deterrence operations in the Arctic.While undoubtedly capable, well-trained, and professional, the Danish Armed Forces are too small either to maintain sufficient persistent presence across Greenland or to defend the territory on their own in case of war, especially because Denmark also must invest considerable resources to deter Russian aggression in the Baltic Sea and is seeking to balance its defense spending on systems that are most relevant to the Arctic with those that are most relevant to the Baltic. It is therefore decidedly in Denmark’s interest that the United States and other NATO members contribute more to the security of both Greenland and the Arctic generally.Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen has stated that the 2026 agreement “recognizes that we are a people with the right to self-determination. At the same time, we are recognized as a part of our common security in the Arctic.”[REF] Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has likewise stated that:Today, we have signed a good agreement. For Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States. And for NATO and Europe. The agreement strengthens our common defence and security. And it is deeply rooted in the NATO Alliance. The agreement acknowledges and respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.[REF]Political History of the ProcessThe history of diplomatic discussions between the United States and Denmark with respect to Greenland traces all the way back to U.S. Secretary of State William Seward, who purchased Alaska from the Russian Empire in 1867 and explored a similar purchase of Greenland.[REF] Later, the U.S. purchased what became the U.S. Virgin Islands from Denmark in the 1916 Convention between the United States and Denmark for the Cession of the Danish West Indies and proposed at roughly the same time to acquire Greenland as well. Denmark declined to include Greenland in the sale, and in a declaration signed with the convention, the U.S. stated that it would “not object to the Danish Government extending their political and economic interests to the whole of Greenland.”[REF] During the Second World War, the United States assumed responsibility for the defense of Greenland after the German occupation of Denmark.[REF]Following the war, the U.S. again expressed interest in Greenland, and negotiations between Washington and Copenhagen over Greenland’s future security architecture culminated with the 1951 Defense Agreement.[REF] This deal enabled the U.S. to build and operate bases in Greenland.[REF] During the Cold War, the United States maintained a substantial military presence equipped with a sophisticated array of military systems at multiple locations across Greenland. After the Cold War ended, as the United States and Europe de-emphasized great-power competition and defense budgets fell across NATO, the United States closed all but one installation in Greenland, leaving only Pituffik Space Base (originally Thule Air Base). Several amending protocols to the initial 1951 Defense Agreement have been signed since then, but the most consequential prior to 2026 was the 2004 supplemental agreement, which officially included the Greenlandic government as a party to the accord.[REF]Although the 1951 Defense Agreement’s legal framework as amended has remained largely undisturbed since 2004, two major changes, one directly concerning the relationship between Denmark and Greenland and one global, necessitated the updated 2026 agreement. The first was the June 12, 2009, Act on Greenland Self-Government, under which the decision for or against independence is acknowledged to be the right of the people of Greenland; an independence agreement with Denmark then requires the consent of Greenland’s parliament, a referendum in Greenland, and the consent of the Danish parliament.[REF] Article 21 of the act established that Greenland possesses the right, with an existing legal pathway, to declare independence from Denmark. The Preamble to the new agreement signed on September 22, 2026, succinctly captures the need to address this shift, “[n]oting that the procedure for Greenlandic independence is set out in Article 21 of Act no. 473 of 12 June 2009 on Greenland Self-Government.”[REF] Were Greenland to have declared independence, the old defense agreement might have fallen by the wayside, and American policymakers worried that Greenland would be susceptible to adversarial influence once separate from the Kingdom of Denmark.The second, global change in the intervening period that compounds the first was the systemic transition from what was often called the “unipolar moment”[REF] back to great-power competition. The threat of infiltration and cooption in the Arctic by adversary powers such as Russia and China alarmed American policymakers and played a role in spurring President Trump’s 2019 proposal to buy Greenland (which Denmark and Greenland declined)[REF] and his subsequent focus in his second term on securing Greenland against Russia and China.[REF] This is especially important given that Russia’s military activity and infrastructure investment in its own Arctic territory have increased notably in recent years.[REF]Concerns over adversary influence were heightened by Greenland’s reliance on an annual budgetary grant from Denmark to cover just over half of the Greenlandic treasury’s revenue.[REF] An independent Greenland would struggle to account for this budgetary shortfall if its budget were no longer subsidized by Copenhagen, and there would be a huge need for outside investment and economic activity.Elsewhere in the world, China has displayed an opportunistic approach to disbursing and leveraging capital in similar instances, providing debt-trap loans and then seizing infrastructure as payment when the country accepting the Chinese loan is unable to pay.[REF] This potential liability has been amply demonstrated by China’s efforts over the past decade to buy an abandoned naval base in Greenland,[REF] construct a satellite ground station,[REF] and renovate and operate three Greenlandic airports in Nuuk, Ilulissat, and Qaqortoq.[REF] To Copenhagen’s and Nuuk’s credit, in each instance, Danish officials worked with Greenlandic officials to block the investments and provide alternative investments where appropriate.President Trump brought the American concern over these liabilities to the public’s attention in March 2025 when he stated in an address to Congress that “[w]e need Greenland for national security and even international security. And we’re working with everybody involved to try and get it. But we need it really for international world security. And I think we’re going to get it. One way or the other, we’re going to get it.”[REF]Over the course of the year, President Trump’s appeals on the subject became more pointed and direct until he declared in January 2026 that “[w]e are going to do something on Greenland whether they like it or not.”[REF] This prompted a January 14, 2026, meeting in Washington at which Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio met the Danish and Greenlandic foreign ministers and they agreed to establish a high-level trilateral working group to find a compromise solution.[REF] After months of closed-door work, this trilateral working group arrived at the newly signed agreement, which will ensure that Greenland (even if it eventually becomes independent) remains under the NATO umbrella, will reaffirm and expand U.S. forces’ access, and will review and protect critical sectors from adversaries’ investments and control.Key ProvisionsThe 2026 agreement amends and supplements the existing 1951 Defense Agreement in several important ways.Expanded U.S. Military Presence and Access. The agreement expands the U.S. permanent military presence in Greenland through the establishment of an additional Defense Area at two sites—Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig—bringing the total number of U.S. sites in Greenland to three. Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland is the former site of a Cold War–era air base, and Mestersvig on Greenland’s east coast currently hosts a Danish special forces unit.[REF] The United States will also be allowed to modernize and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base. The United States committed to awarding construction, maintenance, and servicing contracts to local Greenlandic companies to the maximum extent possible.The agreement also augments existing free movement rights for U.S. forces and explicitly grants U.S. public vessels undersea access within Greenland’s territorial waters “without restriction except as mutually agreed upon by the Parties.”[REF]Establishment of Military Installations by Non-NATO States. The updated agreement adds a prohibition of “manned or unmanned military installations by third states” unless otherwise agreed, intended to exclude Russia and China from ever establishing a presence in Greenland.[REF]Strategic Investment. The recent agreement’s most novel provision, Article X, concerns foreign direct investment in strategic projects (“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” in the agreement).[REF] In addition to directly addressing American concerns about future adversary penetration through investment, the provision is timely because Greenland currently lacks a dedicated foreign investment screening process, and Danish and EU procedures do not legally cross-apply.[REF] The agreement specifies that:[S]tates or investors from a state that is not a member of NATO, a NATO partner, or an EU member state shall not be allowed to have (i) control, (ii) significant influence, or (iii) access to non-public information that may constitute a threat to national security or public order within Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities in the territory of Greenland (including the Territorial Waters), unless agreed between the Parties that the activities of such states or investors would not constitute a threat to national security or public order.[REF]“Particularly Sensitive Sectors or Activities” is defined for purposes of the agreement as “including but not limited to critical infrastructure and the extraction of resources,”[REF] and the implicated provision explicitly includes Greenland’s territorial waters within the area of consideration.[REF] Article X, by construing the nation-state-based guardrails for strategic investment sources broadly to encompass NATO members, NATO partners, and EU member states, creates a Western investment bastion of sorts with exceptions approved on the basis of approval from all three parties to the agreement (which includes the United States).[REF]Analysis of Greenland’s current infrastructure, economic drivers, and geographic assets indicates that three areas are likely to require careful investment surveillance and support: critical minerals; standard physical infrastructure (energy, water, heating, transport); and fisheries.Greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.The combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese company to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build new airports in Greenland.[REF]Permanence. One of the most important features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF]ConclusionThe American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    Sources indicate that president Donald Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a major achievement that will have positive security outcomes for the United States far into the foreseeable future. The agreement will also improve Danish and Greenlandic security, increase American military contributions to Arctic security, strengthen Greenland’s role in the transatlantic security architecture, and ensure that there is no risk of adversarial malign influence even if Greenland’s political status changes. From both the American and European perspectives, the agreement cements and expands the U.S. role in Arctic security, primarily through the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and signals sustained American interest in transatlantic cooperation on Arctic security for many years to come.

    In a recent development, critics have claimed that the deal is the same as before and that the upcoming agreement does not provide anything the United States did not have before, which is demonstrably untrue.[REF] The 2026 agreement augments, updates, and improves the existing 1951 Defense Agreement: expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with new defense areas at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig that will host U.S. troops, creating a new mechanism for the prohibition of Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and establishing a process for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk, and Washington to bar investment by non-allied states in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy such as the mining sector, ports, and airports.[REF].

    The fresh agreement’s provisions would continue to apply even if Greenland were to become independent.

    The agreement details the core U.S. national security interests at stake and the rationale behind the push for an expanded agreement, “[r]ecognizing the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and “[n]oting that the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”[REF].

    Industry observers note that the strategic rationale for American interest in securing Greenland from adversarial influence and maintaining a military presence is enduring, rational, and grounded in more than a century of U.S. strategic thinking.[REF] It is strongest when considered in the context of great-power competition and homeland defense, as the Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) heading toward the U.S. and Greenland in particular lies on the shortest and most likely path for these systems when they are fired from Russia.[REF] During the Cold War, both the United States and the Soviet Union operated submarines under the polar ice cap, tested weapons, and invested heavily in surveillance and early warning systems across the land, air, sea, and undersea domains because of the same geographic and strategic realities.

    Industry observers note that greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland–Iceland–U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass.[REF] It is crucial for the United States and its NATO allies to maintain awareness of Russian and Chinese submarines passing through this area, especially ballistic missile submarines equipped with nuclear weapons.

    According to recent reports, the airspace above Greenland is also critically key to defending the U.S. homeland, as U.S. military radars in Greenland contribute to the detection of any hostile ballistic missile movements toward North America.[REF] Because the Arctic is the shortest path between Russia and the United States and between China and the United States, Russian ICBMs, strategic bombers, and hypersonic and cruise missiles would most likely traverse the Arctic on course for the U.S. in the event of a war—a fact that led Washington to negotiate the 1951 Defense Agreement with Denmark early in the Cold War. North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), a binational U.S.–Canada command, requires persistent Arctic and High North domain awareness to fulfill its core mission of defending the continent’s airspace.[REF] During the Cold War, the U.S. had an extended network of manned radar installations across the Arctic known as the Distant Early Warning Line (DEW Line), but it closed much of this network during the 1990s after the Cold War ended.[REF] The U.S. also operated a series of air and naval bases across Greenland that were likewise closed during the 1990s.

    Today, with the return of great-power competition with China and Russia, Washington has recognized the need to rebuild this Arctic infrastructure as an essential element of continental defense. Pituffik Space Base in Greenland is one of the central nodes in this architecture because its Upgraded Early Warning Radar is one of only a few U.S. or allied sensors providing ballistic missile warning and space surveillance coverage of the North Atlantic and polar approaches to North America.

    In a recent development, the United States is increasing its engagement in the Arctic region in several ways, and the increased U.S. activity in Greenland is closely interconnected with other major national security projects being undertaken by the Trump Administration. For example, in view of the long-standing U.S. icebreaker shortage, Pituffik Space Base currently relies on a Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker for its annual resupply, given the longtime U.S. icebreaker shortage.[REF] The Icebreaker Collaboration Effort, or ICE Pact, seeks to remedy this shortage by building a much larger U.S. fleet of icebreakers in collaboration with Finland and Canada.[REF] The Trump Administration’s Golden Dome initiative to defend the North American continent from missile threats likewise has a major Arctic component and is mentioned in the Greenland agreement’s preamble as one of the shared interests of the three parties.[REF].

    Industry observers note that greenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It enjoys a significant degree of self-rule, but responsibility for defense and foreign policy remains primarily with the Danish government in Copenhagen.

    The newly introduced agreement recognizes the shared interest of the United States, Denmark, and Greenland in “allowing the United States to have military access to the territory of Greenland to the extent necessary to defend the North Atlantic Treaty area, Greenland, and the American continent, including through establishment of a Golden Dome defense system.”[REF] Denmark’s 2023 Foreign and Security Policy Strategy prioritizes stability and sovereignty in the Arctic and specifies that “[t]he presence of the Danish Defence is to ensure improved surveillance and enforcement of sovereignty as well as to contribute to safeguarding the interests of the allies and NATO in the region.”[REF].

    Recent findings suggest that china has demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region. Chinese investments, for example, have targeted Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.[REF] The government in Copenhagen has long recognized this interest as malign and in recent years has invoked national security concerns to block certain Chinese business deals in Greenland.[REF].

    In 2025, Denmark committed billions to systems and infrastructure relevant to Arctic security, particularly the defense of Greenland.[REF] This commitment included a spending package with two fresh Arctic vessels, a regional headquarters based in Nuuk, and additional maritime patrol aircraft.[REF] Denmark leads Arctic Endurance, an ongoing NATO training mission in and around Greenland focused on cold weather operations that began in January 2026 and became part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry a month later.[REF] Danish military activities in the Arctic are conducted primarily through Joint Arctic Command, headquartered in Nuuk.[REF].

    It has been revealed that denmark has long been a reliable and capable U.S. ally and member of NATO. Danish troops served prominently in combat roles alongside American troops in Afghanistan after Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty was invoked in response to the September 11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates among NATO allies.[REF] Denmark spent 3.2 percent of gross domestic product on defense as of 2025—one of the highest percentages in the NATO alliance—and is projected to be among the first NATO allies to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the very near future.[REF] Much of Denmark’s latest spending will be to procure high-end capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory in Greenland.[REF].

    The Danish Navy operates Iver Huitfeldt–class air defense frigates and Absalon-class frigates, as well as patrol vessels of varying capabilities.[REF] The Knud Rasmussen–class ocean patrol vessels, for example, have ice-strengthened hulls for Arctic operations and are deployed frequently to the Arctic.[REF] In 2026, Denmark announced a shipbuilding strategy that included the production of five upcoming Arctic ships for the Danish Navy.[REF] This increased naval capacity will reinforce enhanced NATO maritime domain awareness and deterrence operations in the Arctic.

    Industry observers note that while undoubtedly capable, well-trained, and professional, the Danish Armed Forces are too small either to maintain sufficient persistent presence across Greenland or to defend the territory on their own in case of war, especially because Denmark also must invest considerable resources to deter Russian aggression in the Baltic Sea and is seeking to balance its defense spending on systems that are most relevant to the Arctic with those that are most relevant to the Baltic. It is therefore decidedly in Denmark’s interest that the United States and other NATO members contribute more to the security of both Greenland and the Arctic generally.

    Greenland possesses substantial geological reserves of rare earth elements with 1.5 million tons of proven reserves and an estimated 36 million tons of total resources, putting it among the world’s top 10 countries in terms of geological assets. Greenland also possesses substantial uranium deposits as well as many other non–rare earth minerals with wide commercial applications.[REF] However, two principal difficulties—ice and regulation—will slow the pace of investment and development. The Greenland Ice Sheet extends across 656,000 square miles (roughly 80 percent of the country) and reaches thicknesses of more than 1.9 miles, making any significant extraction operation extremely complicated.[REF] With respect to regulation, Greenland banned uranium mining in 2021 and banned exploration of mineral deposits with even low levels (100 parts per million) of uranium, which caused a halt to a major rare earth mine because of colocation of minerals.[REF] If these difficulties are overcome, Western investment in Greenland could bring major secure upstream production of rare earth elements online.

    The combination of a small population and a harsh and geographically isolating environment has caused the majority of Greenlandic communities to function independently with nearly no road networks apart from a few that link sheep farms in southern Greenland. Because of the difficulties involved in providing such essentials as power, water, and heating, these needs are serviced by a combination of national and local government entities.[REF] Therefore, any investment by non-allied nations in these utilities should be subject to Article X’s provisions because communities could effectively be held hostage if provision of these services were to be interrupted or maintenance were to be delayed.

    Finally, fisheries deserve attention with respect to critical investments in Greenland not only because they represent the primary national industry, but also because of the vital economic lifeline they provide for certain settlement economies.[REF] In addition, trends in ice distribution appear likely to herald an increase in fishing grounds off West Greenland that could spur economic growth in this sector.[REF] These economic opportunities could cement their outsized importance to the Greenlandic economy as consumer demand for seafood is expected to rise for decades;[REF] therefore, these benefits should be retained for local producers and fair partners.

    It should be noted that Denmark has already proven itself to be highly cooperative in this regard, having blocked the aforementioned attempt by a Chinese firm to purchase the abandoned Grønnedal naval base as well as another attempt by China to build latest airports in Greenland.[REF].

    Industry observers note that permanence. One of the most key features of the updated 2026 agreement is that it addresses concern arising from the potential impact of Greenlandic independence by establishing that the agreement allowing the U.S. military presence, prohibiting non-NATO military bases, and establishing a mechanism for excluding malign investment by non-NATO governments will endure even if Greenland becomes independent. Specifically, the agreement provides that:.

    In case Greenland exercises its right to self-determination to become independent, the Government of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Government of Greenland shall together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will (i) agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary, and (ii) affirmatively assume, as from the date of independence, all of the rights and obligations of the Kingdom of Denmark specified in this Agreement, including any implementation agreements or arrangements between the Parties, as well as the Defense Arrangements.[REF].

    The American, Danish, and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure and sovereign Arctic where the shortest approaches to North America from Russia and China are secured and the rights of all Arctic states are respected. The September 2026 agreement protects the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps to ensure transatlantic security cooperation through NATO in the Arctic for decades to come.[REF] This major diplomatic achievement expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits non-NATO military presence, protects critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy that otherwise could have been exploited for dual-use purposes by adversarial governments, and permanently cements Greenland’s status and role in transatlantic security.

    Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Douglas and Sarah Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation. Jordan Embree is a Senior Research Associate in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation.

    “It’s the economy, stupid.” That 1992 catchphrase by Bill Clinton advisor James Carville is being repeated in the aftermath of the Republican debacle last week. And it’s true that the economy can never be ignored. But “it’s the culture, stupid,” is a more apt refrain.

    People, especially the young, voted nearly 10 socialists into the U.S. Congress, and socialists will now lead four of our largest and most crucial cities: New York, Los Angeles, Seattle, and our capital.

    How did that happen in the Land of the Free, a country that used to have an in-built immunity to Marxism? Students for two or more generations have been acculturated to believe that Marxism is good and America is bad.

    Professors at these universities had to work assiduously. Americans’ resistance to Marxism used to be so strong that, according to urban legend, Soviet tyrant Josef Stalin was the first to coin the term “American exceptionalism” as he decried American imperviousness to the siren song of communism.

    Industry observers note that in June 1929, Jay Lovestone, leader of the Communist Party USA, visited Moscow to meet Stalin, and told him that the American worker was not interested in revolution. America’s lack of a feudal past, as well as other national character traits, made Americans inherently resistant. Stalin shot back that he was tired of this “heresy of American exceptionalism.”.

    >>> No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability.

    That account, coming from Stalin’s biographers and popularized by the Atlantic, has been disputed, and Alexis de Tocqueville had already described the United States as “exceptional” in Democracy in America in 1835. But the story illustrates an important point. America is exceptional in many important ways—like its unique adherence to Natural Right—but no longer when it comes to being immune to socialism.

    Voters last week elected six new members of the Democratic Socialists of America to the House of Representatives: Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-NY); Claire Valdez (D-NY); Melat Kiros (D-CO); Donavan McKinney (D-MI); Chris Rabb (D-PA); and Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-CA).

    This freshman class joins Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), both first elected in 2018, and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who describes himself as a democratic socialist but is technically an independent.

    And of course, there is the upcoming Mayor of Washington, D.C., Janeese Lewis George, who won 84% of the vote on Election Day, and Nithya Raman, the new mayor of Los Angeles, both proud socialists.

    Industry observers note that the economy was the No. 1 reason voters gave for voting the way they did. Four in 10 voters named the economy, and 90% mentioned the cost of living was a crucial factor, according to The World Data.

    Industry observers note that color me skeptical. I agree more with economist Steve Moore, who stated on Fox News last Friday, after a stellar jobs report that beat expectations by a factor of 10,.

    I wish that would have come out a week ago, I mean, it could have changed things a lot. And by the way, I wrote a column the day after the election saying it wasn’t about ‘the economy, stupid,’ because the economy is pretty damn strong. I mean, you see it, everything that you all have been saying about what’s going on with construction, with manufacturing, with low unemployment rate, the fact there are more jobs than workers.

    Recent findings suggest that indeed, GDP is growing at an annualized rate of 3.4% in the last quarter. Private domestic demand is even stronger, rising almost 5%, the fastest in five years. The unemployment rate sits at 4.1%, and layoffs remain low.

    It has been revealed that so, why are the voters so upset? It is true that young white males (a key Trump constituency in 2024) are having a tougher time, with the economy churning out more jobs that are geared to women, and because of discrimination against them due to diversity, equity, and inclusion targets, which continue despite Trump’s best efforts. These voters are facing real pressure points: housing, student debt, gas, groceries, etc.

    According to recent reports, the Democrats were also disciplined in their messaging and had a great media ground game. The activist Van Jones explained on CNN that Democratic operatives had a coordinated social media campaign that involved tens of thousands of people acting through the “American Accountability Network,” a lefty consortium of content creators.

    >>> The Surprising Latest Guardians Of Liberty And What It Means For The Left.

    “The Republicans never figured out what we were doing,” said Jones, who, according to the writer Eitan Fischberger, claimed that this campaign generated 32.5 million daily hits on Instagram, 88.8 million on X and 185 million on Facebook, “driving the kitchen table affordability message and tying that to Democrats on a positive and Republicans on a negative.”.

    That voters then chose candidates with a socialist economic agenda that won’t address existing problems and has failed everywhere it’s been tried lies squarely on the capture by Marxists of the cultural institutions. Why do 60% of Democrats have a favorable view of socialism? They have been indoctrinated by the universities, the schools, the museums, the media, etc.

    Just ask conductor Andris Nelsons, who the Boston Symphony Orchestra fired as part of its ill-advised search for “relevance.” Nelsons brought increased ticket sales, but he was not aligned with the more “inclusive” direction the BSO is misguidedly taking.

    As Heather Mac Donald wrote on City Journal, “The main point of contention between the board and Nelsons … seems to have been the conductor’s allegedly inadequate enthusiasm for the race- and gender-based programming and hiring that became so dominant in the classical music world after the George Floyd riots.”.

    Any conservative who ignores all this, takes Carville to heart, looks at the election results and concludes that all the attention must be trained on the economy, to the exclusion of the oft-derided “culture wars,” will be making a significant mistake.

    • The case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S.
    • The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial issues was more of a First Amendment matter, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The eastern facade of the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School in 2006. (Photo by Jeffrey M. Vinocur, CC-BY-SA-3.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

    The case of a suspended professor at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School who claims that she was fired because of her race after making comments about minority groups would be better considered as a free speech matter, a panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Philadelphia stated Tuesday.

    The three-judge panel in Philadelphia suggested that professor Amy Wax’s claims of retaliation for speaking about racial issues was more of a First Amendment matter, rather than employment discrimination, as she had argued.

    In her brief, Wax, a white Jewish woman, stated that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1981 of the Civil Rights Act prohibit discrimination “on the ground of race” and “on the basis of race,” respectively, differing them from Title VII.

    She argued that the the University of Pennsylvania had an alleged double standard, allowing faculty and students to participate in what she called antisemitic demonstrations against Israel without consequences but punishing her for her commentary on race.

    #101543. Second Amendment as a Right to Sell Guns as Well as to Have and Buy Them?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2032 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Second Amendment as a Right to Sell Guns as Well as to Have and Buy Them?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S.
    • Jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C.
    • Sources indicate that the district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S. v. Deare:.

    Jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(a)(1) and for making false statements with respect to records of licensed firearms dealers. Deare then filed a motion to dismiss the indictment, broadly challenging the constitutionality of § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements.

    Sources indicate that the district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms. The court further held that, even if federal licensing requirements are implicated by the Second Amendment, such requirements are consistent with our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation….

    Industry observers note that deare primarily challenges the district court's denial of his motion to dismiss the indictment. Specifically, he argues that the Second Amendment's plain text covers firearm sales, and that § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements are inconsistent with our Nation's history of firearm regulation.

    The plain text of the Second Amendment covers the sale of firearms. As we noted in Reese v. BATFE (5th Cir. 2025), "the right to 'keep and bear arms' surely implies the right to purchase them." During oral argument, the government conceded that the Second Amendment applies to the commercial sale of firearms.

    Accordingly, we vacate the district court's order denying Deare's motion to dismiss the indictment and remand to the district court for further proceedings.

    (As I read the opinion, it doesn't affect the false statements charge.).

    It's gratifying that our court today reaffirms what we should have long understood—that the Second Amendment right to "keep and bear Arms" plainly encompasses the sale of arms as well. It seems obvious that constitutional rights are meaningless if the Government can simply prohibit the means by which citizens are able to exercise those rights.

    Our dissenting colleague theorizes that 18 U.S.C. § 922(a) is not about constitutional rights, but about commercial regulation. It's the same view expressed by the district court below: "§ 922(a)(1) is a modest regulation of the commercial activity of selling/transferring firearms to others…. [F]ederal licensure and record keeping requirements do not affect an individual's rights to possess firearms…. [T]hese requirements affect only the seller. As such, Defendants have failed to persuade this Court that these commercial licensure and recordkeeping requirements implicate the Second Amendment.".

    Or as the dissent puts it simply, "the Second Amendment … doesn't mention sellers," so "I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered.".

    According to recent reports, by that logic, the First Amendment doesn't mention sellers, so presumably booksellers aren't covered by the First Amendment, either. But that can't be right.

    It has been revealed that constitutional rights are constitutional rights, regardless of whether they're compensated—as I've noted on a number of occasions. And if that's true under the First Amendment, then it should be equally true in Second Amendment challenges to § 922(a) as well….

    Our dissenting colleague responds by offering a textual distinction between the First and Second Amendments. At bottom, the dissent theorizes that the "freedom of speech" contemplates sales, whereas "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms" does not. But with respect, I don't see the textual distinction that she sees. The theory is also hard to square with what we saw in Villarreal.….

    Judge Oldham, joined by Judge Ho, concurred in the judgment (though presumably they also joined their own unsigned opinion):.

    It has been revealed that the first question presented is whether restrictions on the sale of firearms burden the Second Amendment rights of American citizens. They do—in at least two ways. First, such restrictions directly burden the seller's right to keep and bear arms. And second, they burden the prospective buyer's right to keep and bear arms, because the right to keep an item always includes the right to acquire it.

    Start with the constitutional text. The Second Amendment does not just prohibit the government from denying the right to keep and bear arms. Instead, it says that the right cannot be "infringed." And at the Founding, "infringe" meant "violate," "destroy," or "hinder." Thus, the government cannot hinder the people's rights to keep and bear arms.

    According to recent reports, restrictions on sale hinder both the seller's and buyer's right to keep and bear arms. Start with the seller's right to possess firearms. The Second Amendment guarantees the right to keep guns for personal use, and the seller is an individual who can lawfully possess guns. And it's hornbook property law that the right to possess an article "includes the right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." So the right to keep a gun must include the right to dispose of that gun as the owner sees fit. This is not an independent "right to sell." Rather, my point is that governmental interference with the right to sell a firearm is itself a burden on the seller's existing property right in that firearm. It hinders and hence infringes the seller's rights.

    The same logic applies to the buyer. The buyer's ability to keep and bear arms is certainly "infringed" by regulations that hinder the purchase of arms. After all, the Supreme Court has explained that inherent in "property" is the "right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." In other words, a restriction on the sale of weapons obviously impacts the buyer's constitutional rights to acquire weapons. As one scholar has explained it:.

    According to recent reports, because one cannot 'keep' or 'bear' something without acquiring it, the act of acquiring arms must be included in the Second Amendment's 'right to keep and bear arms.' This is true for the same reason that the right to speak would be largely ineffective if it did not include the right to engage in financial transactions that are the incidents of its exercise. For there comes a point at which the regulation of action intimately and unavoidably connected with a right is a regulation of the right itself.

    Joseph G.S. Greenlee, The American Tradition of Self-Made Arms, 54 St. Mary's L.J. 35 (2023).

    Sources indicate that this principle is not limited to the Second Amendment context. For example, consider the neighboring First Amendment. The Free Speech Clause "afford[s] the public access to discussion, debate, and the dissemination of information and ideas"—and thus clearly protects the right to sell and distribute speech, including speech written or produced by others. And it protects the recipient's right to receive information and ideas. Willis v. Town of Marshall (9th Cir. 2002) (Kozinski, J., concurring) ("[T]he right to hear and the right to speak are flip sides of the same coin."). Without a right to provide speech, there is no right to receive information and ideas.

    According to recent reports, likewise, consider the Free Exercise Clause. "[T]he text of the Free Exercise Clause gives a specific group of people (those who wish to engage in the 'exercise of religion') the right to do so without hindrance." It is axiomatic that the right to free exercise of religion includes the right to practice it with others in, for example, houses of worship. Shutting down houses of worship is an obvious First Amendment violation for many reasons—not the least of which is that it prevents the faithful from communing with each other and with church leaders who provide teaching, holy sacraments, and other sacred traditions. Thus, the right to exercise religion includes a First Amendment freedom to participate in religious services with—and provide religious services to—others.

    These examples demonstrate clear principles. A right to property, free speech, corporate worship, and firearms includes the right to provide these things. And to acquire them….

    Industry observers note that judge Oldham also discussed the proper scope of a Fifth Circuit decision, U.S. v. Peterson (5th Cir. 2025) and concludes that it (1) "was wrong and should be overturned" and in any event (2) doesn't apply here; for more on that, read the full opinion.

    Judge Catharina Haynes dissented:.

    I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered by the Second Amendment (which doesn't mention sellers) …. {Second Amendment is quite different from the First Amendment mentioned in the concurrence. The First Amendment states "freedom of speech" and lists people in general which is quite large whereas the Second Amendment notes "the right of people to keep and bear Arms" not mentioning selling Arms or all situations.}.

    [But] I am respectful of the majority opinion on that given our prior cases and what the government mentioned. So, even assuming arguendo the sellers are covered, I see nothing in this case that indicates that the rules for the sellers in this context are inappropriate and, therefore, unconstitutional. Also, to me, since Deare did not properly challenge the relevant rules to show that they are abusive, I do not see a need to remand on that. To me, the relevant rules as to him are sufficient and proper, so I would simply affirm.

    I appreciate Judge Ho's and Judge Oldham's arguments that the right to keep and bear arms must include the right to acquire them, which in turn means that restrictions on sales must be evaluated to make sure they don't improperly burden the rights of would-be buyers. By way of analogy, the Court continues to recognize a right to use contraceptives (see Griswold v. Connecticut). Surely that must mean that a ban on selling contraceptives would unconstitutionally burden the would-be buyers' rights, and even less comprehensive restrictions on selling them might likewise be seen as too burdensome.

    But I'm skeptical of the argument that the Second Amendment secures a right of sellers independent of the right of buyers. A bookseller may be said to be engaged in "speech" in the sense that conveying ideas to readers is a form of speech (including when one conveys them in exchange for money). A gun seller, on the other hand, isn't actually "keeping" a gun or "bearing" it. And though property rights do generally include the right to convey, including by sale, I don't think the Second Amendment should be seen as constitutionalizing that.

    By way of analogy, the law bans transferring guns to felons. That, the Court has said, is presumptively constitutional, because felons don't have the right to possess guns (focusing on the rights of the would-be gun possessor). But I don't think it follows that the law even implicates the right of gun sellers. When the law bans me from selling a gun to a felon, it isn't affecting my own ability to keep or bear the gun at all.

    And this distinction between (1) the Second Amendment protecting gun sales as facilitative of the buyer's ability to have a gun, and (2) the Second Amendment gun sales as protecting the seller's own Second Amendment rights, may be practically significant. Under theory 1, there would likely be more room for regulation of sellers, since restrictions that only very modestly affect the buyer's ability to buy guns might then be viewed as presumptively constitutional. (That's consistent with D.C. v. Heller's statement that "nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on … laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms"). Under theory 2, there would be less room for regulation of sellers, since the sellers' own rights would be at stake as well.

    Industry observers note that again, that's also how the distinction might play out as to the right to use contraceptives, and how it played out as to abortion in the pre-Dobbs Roe/Casey era. For instance, the right to abortion was consistent with licensure requirements for people or organizations that perform abortions, so long as this didn't unduly interfere with women's ability to get abortions. Likewise, it seems to me, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms is consistent with licensure requirements for gun sellers, so long as it doesn't unduly interfere with people's ability to get guns that they can then keep and bear.

    Justice Department Announces Actions to Disrupt North Korea’s Massive Theft of Cryptocurrency

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency.
    • Industry observers note that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M.
    • It has been revealed that “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” remarked Assistant Attorney General A.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency. These actions include the seizure of cloud-based infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering scheme that has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency and the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance, a virtual currency exchange.

    Industry observers note that “North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “Today’s announcement reveals that America will fight back against that corrupt regime’s effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains.”.

    It has been revealed that “The Criminal Division, specifically the Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), and our law enforcement partners played the critical role in immediately freezing billions of dollars’ worth of stolen Binance digital assets before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” remarked Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “As the Department’s liaison to the digital asset industry, the Criminal Division promptly and efficiently used its expertise to immediately halt about half of this historic breach.”.

    Industry observers note that “Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”.

    “By springing into action at a moment’s notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets.”.

    “The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years,” stated FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “North Korean cyber actors have used the FaceStealer scheme to aggressively target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors through deceptive social engineering tactics, resulting in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months. The FBI remains committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing cost on North Korean actors targeting the virtual asset community.”.

    Sources indicate that “North Korea’s FaceStealer is a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user” noted Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office. “It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough. The FBI is sounding the alarm to elevate awareness of this growing scheme, now aimed not only at crypto theft, but also the exploitation of the of the open-source software supply chain.”.

    Seizure of FaceStealer Infrastructure – Central District of California.

    Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California unveiled the disruption of cloud-based infrastructure used by North Korean hackers in a highly effective social engineering scheme that the FBI is calling “FaceStealer.” The scheme, which relies on surreptitiously recorded videos and artificial deepfakes, has resulted in the theft of more than $400 million in the last 18 months and the attempted compromise of individuals involved in the open-source software supply chain.

    It has been revealed that north Korean hackers known publicly by the names Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, Advanced Persistent Threat 38 (APT38), BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima have lured targets with invitations to video meetings delivered from accounts stolen from prior victims. Once a target joins the meeting, the hackers record the target’s webcam video and play a prerecorded video of a previous victim or victims known to the target, thereby simulating the participation of trusted contacts in the meeting to gain the target’s trust. The North Korean hackers also use super intelligence (SI) to develop deepfake videos of well-known and influential individuals often in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries that make the FaceStealer scheme even more effective. Here again, they use the deepfake videos in the meetings with targets to gain the target’s trust.

    During the meeting, the hackers then introduce a fake technical error into the meeting, such as claiming that the target cannot be heard, and provide a link or prompt to fix the error. The “fix” surreptitiously installs malware on the target’s computer. With the target’s computer compromised, the hackers can steal cryptocurrency or exploit the target’s access to other computer infrastructure. In several reported cases, the hackers stole cryptocurrency and hijacked communication accounts several months to more than a year after the initial compromise. As part of the scheme the hackers also accessed the new victim’s contact lists, social media, and communications apps to target the victim’s personal and professional contacts.

    Sources indicate that the North Korean hackers target individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries. Additionally, they have increasingly targeted individuals involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software with the FaceStealer technique, attempting to gain access to their devices and the software repository accounts they control. This targeting appears calculated to enable software supply-chain attacks. Pursuant to a federal warrant, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos of FaceStealer victims.

    The FBI today published a report providing greater detail on the mechanics of the FaceStealer scheme, including best practices to protect against this scheme and steps victims can take in the event of a compromise. Additionally, the FBI created a website, www.fbi.gov/facestealer, to serve as a centralized hub for resources and information on the scheme.

    According to recent reports, the effort to disrupt the FaceStealer campaign was led by Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki for the Central District of California and the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

    The Department, FBI, and Law Enforcement Partners Interdict More Than a Billion Dollars Worth of Virtual Assets Stolen From Binance.

    Separately from the FaceStealer campaign, on or about Oct. 29, members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as “TraderTraitor” stole more than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from the Binance cryptocurrency exchange. Since the theft, the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section, the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and law enforcement partners have worked closely with virtual asset service providers (VASPs) to interdict the stolen assets. Collective U.S. government and private sector efforts so far have resulted in the freeze of more than $2.7 billion, with the Department having already obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount.

    Efforts to trace, freeze, seize, and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder such assets through various cryptocurrency bridges, mixers, and exchanges. For example, last week, the FBI, in coordination with its law enforcement partners at the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS-CI), issued a Cyber Alert attributing the theft and urging VASPs to block transactions with or derived from cryptocurrency addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder the stolen Binance assets.

    The FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office, Cyber Division, and Virtual Asset Unit are coordinating the FBI’s efforts to recover the stolen virtual assets, working in partnership with the USSS and the IRS-CI.
