    #101541. Tech Report: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1689 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.
    • The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.
    • Sources indicate that during the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

    The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:.

    Sources indicate that during the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

    The State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

    Sources indicate that the district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

    In a recent development, we conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

    Industry observers note that the enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

    Through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

    Judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:.

    In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and new parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

    Sources indicate that on May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:.

    Recent findings suggest that 1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

    H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

    Section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

    It has been revealed that at issue here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

    Even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

    After the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

    The $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

    Texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

    I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a fresh requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

    Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:.

    Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

    Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

    It has been revealed that I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

    Sources indicate that the petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the upcoming Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

    More from Derek Muller on Election Law Blog.

    November 18, 2026, 10:34 am CST.

    In a recent development, A former Motley Rice attorney was sentenced Monday in Charleston, South Carolina, to 87 months in prison and ordered to pay more than $2.5 million in restitution. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A former Motley Rice attorney was sentenced Monday in Charleston, South Carolina, to 87 months in prison and ordered to pay more than $2.5 million in restitution for defrauding the law firm through fictitious companies and ‌false settlement claims.

    William Christopher Swett, 42, had previously pleaded guilty to four counts of ​wire fraud and four counts of money laundering, according to a story by Reuters.

    A lawyer ​at South Carolina-based ⁠Motley Rice for 12 years, Swett had a severe gambling addiction and substance abuse issues, according to court papers filed on his behalf.

    Prosecutors have alleged that Swett profited for years ⁠by creating fictitious legal services companies that received reimbursements from Motley Rice. In addition, he allegedly filed fake personal injury claims for family members and put the proceeds into bank accounts that he controlled.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • In a recent development, emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May.
    • “Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” noted Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that (Beirut) – Emirati authorities have arbitrarily detained at least five Shia Muslim foreign residents since the United States and Israel carried out military strikes on Iran in February 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The detentions appear to be based on the detainees’ religious identity.

    In a recent development, emirati authorities detained the residents, who had been in the UAE between 2 and 40 years, between March and May. They have not been brought before a judge or formally charged, three informed sources said.

    “Emirati authorities appear to be rounding up residents simply based on their religious beliefs as Shia Muslims in a largely Sunni country rather than providing any evidence of wrongdoing, while trampling over people’s due process rights,” noted Joey Shea, senior UAE researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately release anyone targeted because of their religion.”.

    Industry observers note that between September and October, Human Rights Watch interviewed the three sources and reviewed CCTV footage of a raid on the company that one of the detainees owned. The detainees’ and sources’ names are withheld for fear of reprisals against them and their relatives.

    Recent findings suggest that the sources said that security authorities asked at least one of the detainees about his religious affiliation before his arrest and interrogated at least one family member about their religious views. Another Shia community member warned at least one detainee and a relative to leave the UAE.

    On March 23, Emirati state security arrested one man, 44, in Sharjah, as he was in his car near his home at midnight, a relative noted. He was not allowed to contact a lawyer or his family that night.

    The following night, Emirati security forces took the man to his family home for a search. The officers took money, jewelry, books, and credit cards, his relative stated. Security forces did not inform him or his family of any charges against him.

    It has been revealed that the relative said that a worker at the mosque they attended had warned him to leave the country in June 2025. The government “viewed us Shias as sleeper cells,” he said. The relative left the UAE two days later.

    The same mosque worker asked the man on March 20, 2026, whether he had “any problems with the police.” The relative said this was how the man had been warned, but he did not understand it as a warning and stayed in the UAE.

    Recent findings suggest that emirati security forces also raided the man’s company. Human Rights Watch reviewed CCTV footage reportedly from the site, timestamped March 24. The footage indicates two men, one in a baseball cap and the other in traditional clothing, entering the man’s company at around 9:19 p.m. and searching offices. One enters a room with computers and appears to tamper with the equipment.

    According to recent reports, the man was held in incommunicado detention for three days, then allowed to make a one-minute call to his family. He has been allowed two-minute calls every two weeks since. Prison authorities end the call if he attempts to reveal information about his case or location. His family has not been allowed to visit.

    According to recent reports, on September 14, the family learned through his lawyer that he had been moved to the notorious al-Sadr prison in Abu Dhabi, the source mentioned. Emirati authorities have held the prominent Emirati human rights defender Ahmed Mansour there since 2017 in conditions that may amount to torture.

    It has been revealed that on the evening of April 22, state security officials arrested a 38-year-old foreign Shia national at a money transfer office near his home in Sharjah, a relative said. They took him to his home and searched it, seizing money, gold jewelry, and his laptop without informing his family of any charges.

    According to recent reports, on May 29, Emirati authorities summoned his wife for questioning, including about her husband’s religious views, the source said. Authorities released her at 10 a.m. on May 30.

    In a recent development, emirati authorities held him in incommunicado detention, allowing him to make a brief call on June 3, the source mentioned. Authorities allow him one brief phone call every week in which he cannot reveal the details of his detention. The authorities told his wife on October 6 that he had been moved to al-Sadr prison. She has not been allowed to visit him.

    Sources indicate that emirati authorities arrested three more foreign Shia nationals between April and May, a third source related to the men stated. Security forces raided the homes of all three men, confiscated their passports and money, and did not inform them of the charges against them, the source said.

    Industry observers note that during one of the raids, a security officer asked a family member about their religion, job, and income, the source remarked. Before the arrest, one of the men received a phone call from Emirati authorities asking about a religious concern and the names of his associates, the source said.

    The three men have been allowed to make a brief call every ten days without revealing their location, the source stated. Prison authorities end the call if they attempt to give details about the case or detention conditions.

    In a recent development, “We all left the UAE in one day,” a family member said. “We wrapped up over 30 years in the UAE… We gave the UAE our hopes, dreams, and children. We sang their national anthem in schools. We loved this country.”.

    Human Rights Watch has previously documented Emirati authorities arbitrarily detaining and forcibly disappearing and expelling other Shia residents, without due process, between 2009 and 2021. Reuters reported that thousands of Pakistani Shia residents have been deported from Gulf Arab states since February 28. During the same period, Emirati authorities revoked visas of Iranian families who have lived in the UAE for decades and banned Iranian nationals from transiting through the UAE, media and UAE Foreign Ministry reports remarked.

    It has been revealed that on February 28, the United States and Israel carried out airstrikes on Iran, and Iran retaliated with strikes against Israel and Gulf states. Iran has since debuted thousands of drones and missiles at Gulf countries, with the largest number striking the UAE. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International found that Gulf governments responded by intensifying restrictions on the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly during the conflict, in an already repressive environment.

    It has been revealed that under international law, governments have a responsibility to protect public safety in wartime, but security measures must be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and nondiscriminatory. Detaining people because of their religion and holding them without charge and access to lawyers is never justified, Human Rights Watch stated.

    “Emirati authorities should not treat the Shia community as a security threat in response to Iran’s unlawful strikes on the UAE,” Shea noted.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats.
    • Since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people.
    • The judge said the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that between August 28 and September 16, US military forces intercepted and destroyed eight Ecuadorian fishing vessels, alleging that they served as floating refueling stations for drug-trafficking boats. They detained 146 of the 160 crew members and transferred them to Ecuadorian authorities, who charged 90 with “unlawful association.”.

    Since Human Rights Watch reported on the operations, Ecuadorian courts have acquitted 40 people. In an October 29 judgment reviewed by Human Rights Watch, a Manta judge acquitted eight fishermen from a vessel named the Don Rufo. The prosecution’s own witnesses, including Ecuadorian police and Navy officials, testified that no illicit items were recovered, and that they knew of no prior investigation linking the fishermen to organized crime.

    The judge said the prosecution rested on a “chain of successive presumptions.” He admonished the prosecutor for pursuing an unsupported case and closed it.

    Industry observers note that the ruling follows an October 7 decision acquitting another 32 crew members from the Conquista II and María Candelaria on similar grounds. The judge found no evidence supporting the unlawful association charge and admonished prosecutors for pursuing the case without even minimal evidence.

    Sources indicate that out of the 160 crew members intercepted by the US, 110, that is 70 percent, are now free and without charges. Fourteen were not brought before Ecuadorian authorities, 56 were released without charge by a judge, and 40 were acquitted. Fifty others are awaiting trial.

    Neither Ecuador nor the United States has publicly disclosed the operation’s legal basis, including the criteria used to intercept the vessels, and in some cases destroy them, or evidence linking the boats to drug trafficking.

    Recent findings suggest that the US Congress should ensure oversight over these and other US security operations in and near Ecuador, where people have been detained without evidence and, in some cases, tortured by Ecuadorian personnel. Organized crime in Ecuador is a serious threat that should be addressed with an effective and rights respecting security and justice policy, not with human rights violations.

    This article has been updated to reflect the correct number of crew members detained and overall intercepted by US military forces.

    • A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a New York court to dismiss the case.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 11:34 am CST.

    David Beckham poses after he was made a knight bachelor at an investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle on Nov. 4, 2025, in Windsor, England. (Photo by Andrew Matthews/Getty Images).

    A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a New York court to dismiss the case.

    The Associated Press reported Tuesday that German-based Coty has argued that the New York Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction, and that Beckham’s commercial entity DB Ventures is simply using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from their deal to sign with another company.

    DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

    According to the AP, Beckham’s name is a famous global brand synonymous with luxury and elegance.

    “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the complaint noted. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”.

    According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

    It has been revealed that coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent company, declined to comment to the AP.

    Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

    According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

    Philippines: US Tech Hub to Displace Hundreds

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.
    • Recent findings suggest that the Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities.
    • It has been revealed that “Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” stated Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Manila) – The Philippine government’s impending construction of a technology manufacturing hub under the US government’s “Pax Silica” initiative will displace hundreds of Indigenous peoples and farmers in Tarlac province, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.

    Recent findings suggest that the Philippine government will provide the land—including territory inhabited for generations by the Indigenous Aeta tribe—while investors, including US companies, will finance the infrastructure and facilities. The framework agreement between the Philippines and the United States is yet to be signed.

    It has been revealed that “Indigenous communities and small farmers fear they will be unlawfully displaced by the semiconductor hub,” stated Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should follow domestic laws and international standards that protect land rights.”.

    Human Rights Watch visited two affected sites in Capas in October 2026—Sapang Kawayan in Barangay Aranguren and Sitio Binyayan in Barangay O’Donnell—and spoke to 11 residents.

    According to recent reports, pax Silica is a US initiative that began in December 2025 to secure US technology supply chains. Under Pax Silica, the US State Department has brokered agreements with other countries and international entities on issues including mineral extraction, technology hardware manufacturing, communications infrastructure, software and platforms, and trade. The Philippines joined Pax Silica in April 2026 and agreed to host a 1,618-hectare semiconductor hub in the town of Capas in Tarlac province, north of Manila, largely for mineral processing and semiconductor manufacturing.

    According to recent reports, the hub development is led by the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), a Philippine government body created by law in 1992 that owns and administers areas previously used as US military bases, including territory occupied and used by the Aeta communities. The Pax Silica hub will be inside Latest Clark City, a government and residential complex built by BCDA in 2018. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the government was “terribly excited” about Pax Silica.

    Sources indicate that under the 1997 Indigenous Peoples Rights Act (IPRA), Indigenous peoples have the right to lands, inland waters, coastal areas, and natural resources that they have “occupied [and] possessed since time immemorial” and can receive Certificates of Ancestral Domain Title. Extended delays in processing titles have left many Indigenous communities vulnerable to encroachment.

    The Aeta Hungey tribe in Sapang Kawayan has been seeking recognition of its ancestral domain since 1994 and refiled in 1999 after the Indigenous Peoples Rights Act took effect, but has not yet received title.

    In early July 2026, BCDA officials sent letters to Sapang Kawayan residents, informing them that the land they were occupying would be “affected by the project Latest Clark City” and inviting them to discuss it at their Clark office without mentioning the planned hub. These letters and BCDA personnel visits to measure their lands caused immediate concern among residents.

    On July 23, BCDA announced that the hub would be built inside New Clark City.

    Recent findings suggest that chieftain Petronila Capiz-Muñoz remarked that visiting BCDA officials orally informed residents that they will be relocated by December and provided information that left residents worried: “They said the new homes would be 30-square meters per family… We complained; they’d be turning us into a matchbox. We farm here, otherwise how would we have sustained our lives here all this time? We don’t rely on aid.”The former BCDA president, Joshua Bingcang, confirmed to media in September that 40 Aeta Hungey homes would be “pushed a little bit,” affecting about 200 people. BCDA officials told the House of Representatives on November 11 that the relocation site would be in Sitio Binyayan, Barangay O’Donnell, three kilometers from Sapang Kawayan, without access to the streams they use for water.

    According to recent reports, “We do not want to give up our community,” Muñoz said. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.”.

    In a recent development, BCDA has not provided a detailed map, but independent geographers who have been supporting the Aeta have mapped the proposed hub based on available information. It shows Sapang Kawayan inside the hub and Sitio Manabayukan, where a different tribe—the Ayta Mag-Antsi—live, just outside.

    The village head of Barangay O’Donnell, Wendell Mercado, said that he and the mayor of Capas asked BCDA to hold a public consultation. “To this day, we are still waiting,” he said.

    Recent findings suggest that the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples states that Indigenous peoples have the right to participate in decision-making in matters that would affect their rights, and that governments shall seek to obtain their free, prior, and informed consent before adopting measures that may affect them. The declaration also provides that Indigenous peoples shall not be forcibly removed from their lands or territories. Although the declaration is not a binding treaty, the Philippines supported the declaration when the UN General Assembly adopted it in 2007.

    Available information indicates that BCDA never secured the free, prior, and informed consent of Aeta community members, Human Rights Watch said.

    Philippine farmers in Sitio Binyayan have also received BCDA letters and were orally informed that their farmland, but not their homes, would be affected. BCDA confirmed to Mercado in a July 16 letter that 92 “affected persons in the Pax Silica project” live in Barangay O’Donnell, including the farmers in Sitio Binyayan.

    “The farmers called me, confused as to why people were measuring their land, forcing them to sell, giving them 30 days, or 10 days to respond to the offer,” said Mercado. “It’s so cruel.”.

    According to recent reports, the farmers remarked that BCDA officials offered compensation worth 300,000 pesos (about US$4,700) per hectare, which they said they do not want to accept. “I really don’t want to, but what can you do if you’re just a small person who stands alone, what will happen to you?” said Rafael Dela Cruz, a 72-year-old farmer. Mander Matias, another farmer, said he even refused the letter of invitation: “The next time they visited me, there were many of them, six of them, really reiterating they’d take my farmland.”.

    Industry observers note that generations of farmers have lived in Sitio Binyayan, but they have no land titles despite the 1988 Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law, which awards landless farmers the right to collectively own lands they till. The Public Land Act also gives rights to people who have been “in open, continuous, exclusive and notorious possession and occupation of alienable and disposable agricultural lands of the public domain for at least 20 years.”.

    In case of a refusal to take the compensation offer, the right-of-way act states that the government must initiate court expropriation proceedings. “If there’s a way, we will fight so the government won’t take it,” said one farmer.

    Industry observers note that farmers who have cultivated land for generations even without formal ownership may have internationally protected rights and interests in continued use of that land. These touch upon the obligations of states under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, particularly the rights to food and an adequate standard of living. Governments have obligations to recognize and protect legitimate tenure arrangements, prevent arbitrary dispossession, and ensure that any eviction complies with international human rights standards.

    It has been revealed that the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, in a general comment on land rights, stated: “For peasants, access to land and other productive resources is so notable for the realization of most rights under the Covenant that it implies for them a right to land. … It includes the right to have access to, sustainably use and manage land to achieve an adequate standard of living.”.

    The farmers—who have little formal education—fear they do not have the skills for the jobs promised by Pax Silica. “Farming is the only job we know,” stated Wilfredo Gutierrez, 60. Another farmer said that, “Money is temporary; land is forever.”.

    Philippine authorities should protect affected people’s access to land and livelihoods and ensure any agreements made under Pax Silica respect their human rights.

    “The Philippine government shouldn’t be trampling the rights of Indigenous peoples and farmers in its haste to attract foreign technology investment,” Buan said. “Development officials should provide information to people who will be affected and genuinely consult them before proceeding with the hub.”.

    Liberia Lifts a Major Barrier to Education

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a upcoming government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade.
    • Sources indicate that since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban.
    • Parents described the difference the policy was making.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that “Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a upcoming government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

    Sources indicate that since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

    Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”.

    A Human Rights Watch investigation in late 2025 and early 2026 found that registration fees caused severe hardship for many Liberian families and put education out of reach for others. Some parents told us they had delayed enrolling their children for years because they could not afford the fees. Children described being sent home from school over unpaid fees. Others stated they had dropped out of school or turned to child labor.

    The latest policy has the potential to benefit nearly half a million families, helping children start school on time, stay in school, and avoid child labor. But ensuring that all schools comply will be essential. One parent stated that despite the policy, a primary school demanded registration fees for his three children. When he said he couldn't pay, he was told, “No registration, no school.”.

    The government should monitor and enforce compliance with the fee ban, extend the policy to junior and senior secondary schools, and address other costs—including transportation, uniforms, and textbooks—that keep children from attending school.

    Liberia has taken a significant step toward making the right to education a reality for all children, regardless of their financial circumstances. Making education accessible to all children will help reduce inequality and create opportunities for generations to come.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (670 w)

    EU: Countries Strategy Rwanda Deportation Centers

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.
    • Industry observers note that “History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” said Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. The five EU countries confirmed their blueprint to send people whose asylum claims have been rejected in the EU to Rwanda starting in 2027.

    Industry observers note that “History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” said Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch. “The choice of a country that has an abysmal human rights record and resists international scrutiny tracks with that history and evokes deep skepticism that any nominal rights safeguards will be respected.”.

    The recently enacted EU Return Regulation allows member states to set up deportation centers, “return hubs,” in countries outside the EU where people, including families with children, will be sent if they cannot be deported directly to their country of origin. The regulation states that agreements should be reached only with countries that respect international human rights law. Rwanda does not meet this requirement, Human Rights Watch said, yet the five European countries did not provide any human rights or due diligence assessment during the announcement.

    The Rwandan government has a well-established record of repressing dissent, including attacks on rights defenders. Its arrests of critics and dissidents, their ill-treatment in detention, and the government’s interference with the judiciary and failure to investigate suspicious deaths have contributed to a widespread climate of fear and self-censorship. In addition, the Rwandan military provides critical support to and exercises overall control over the M23 armed group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Both Rwandan forces and the M23 are responsible for serious abuses and war crimes.

    It has been revealed that as recently as January, Germany, Greece, Denmark, and the Netherlands raised concerns about Rwanda at its UN human rights review. A similar UK-Rwanda deal raised serious human rights concerns before it was abandoned, an Israel-Rwanda deal led to documented abuse, and the situation of recent deportees from the United States to Rwanda remains largely unknown.

    In addition to the threat of harm to those deported to Rwanda, the deal risks financing and giving political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad, Human Rights Watch noted. It could lead the EU to downplay Rwanda’s problematic human rights record or shy away from pressing for measurable improvements.

    Human Rights Watch has consistently found that deportations to third countries expose people to arbitrary detention, ill-treatment, destitution, and onward returns to harm in their home countries, as well as other serious human rights abuse. The United Nations special rapporteur on the rights of migrants, the Council of Europe commissioner for human rights, and the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights have all cautioned against forcible third-country transfers. The EU countries involved in the deal with Rwanda are bound by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the European Convention on Human Rights.

    According to recent reports, “Forcibly deporting people, including children, to a country where the evidence points to their rights being at risk, is a striking abdication of responsibility and humanity,” Sunderland said. “A deal with Rwanda is likely to cause real harm in addition to not achieving any defensible policy objective.”.

    The photo caption has been updated to include the name of Denmark’s prime minister.

    Bangladesh: Education Crisis for Rohingya Refugee Children

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, (Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch remarked today.
    • Industry observers note that humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps.
    • It has been revealed that “Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” remarked Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, (Bangkok) – Humanitarian education programs for Rohingya refugee children in Bangladesh are struggling amid a collapse in donor funding, Human Rights Watch remarked today. Donors should fully fund the education programs, while Bangladesh should recognize and the United Nations should support a separate Rohingya-led school network.

    Industry observers note that humanitarian education programs have enrolled 312,000 out of approximately 500,000 school-age Rohingya children in the Bangladesh refugee camps. But the programs, which aid cuts had shuttered for months in 2025, are barely adequate even for the children they reach and may close again, humanitarian officials told Human Rights Watch. While resources are shrinking, about 90,000 more refugee children need schooling this year, due to population growth and new arrivals fleeing atrocities in Myanmar. The donor-supported programs have largely ignored the schools that Rohingya teachers set up in the camps, which are well-regarded by refugees for their quality of education, but lack legal status and reach only about 30,000 students.

    It has been revealed that “Donor governments have turned their backs on education for half a million Rohingya students stuck in the world’s largest refugee camp, but so much could be done to mitigate this crisis,” remarked Bill Van Esveld, associate children’s rights director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh should accelerate steps to end bans on education for refugees, and humanitarian agencies should work with the Rohingya-led schools.”.

    On November 19, 2026, the International Court of Justice will deliver its judgment in the case brought by Gambia alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya during the 2016-2017 “clearance operations” constitute genocide and violate the Genocide Convention.

    Bangladesh’s Awami League government, overthrown in 2024, had banned Rohingya children’s access to certified education and higher education in the camps or in the Bangladesh school system. It allowed donor-funded education programs but prohibited Rohingya community-led schools, demolished several, and threatened teachers with exile to Bhasan Char, a remote island.

    The current government has taken positive steps and should lift remaining restrictions on refugees’ access to education amid the donor funding crisis, Human Rights Watch remarked.

    In October, Bangladesh for the first time allowed a few dozen Rohingya primary students to take an internationally recognized primary school examination, supported by the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

    Also for the first time, Bangladesh in October approved a Rohingya nongovernmental organization’s looks to build a primary school in the camps for 240 students and to provide a structured curriculum. The Rohingya Centre UK, set up by the diaspora Rohingya community, remarked that the 10-subject curriculum will be taught from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., significantly more instruction than students receive in donor-funded education programs. The organization is also running training on the new curriculum for other Rohingya-led schools in the camps.

    Teachers in the camps established the Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees in 2025, which now comprises more than 125 community-led schools with up to 30,000 students, and is working to ensure quality education, including standardized exams in the Myanmar curriculum. Establishing the examination board took a year of volunteer outreach in the camps.

    According to recent reports, however, the Bangladesh government has still not accredited any curriculum for Rohingya children, and because community-led schools lack legal status, they cannot receive foreign support directly. As a result, while the UK organization’s school is able to hire and train Rohingya teachers, the project is formally being implemented through a registered Bangladeshi group. Most community-led schools have to charge students small fees to operate, limiting access, and rely on refugees to donate the use of their small living shelters as makeshift classrooms.

    Eight teachers at community-led schools mentioned that to reach more students, they need Bangladesh to grant their schools official status, allow official certification of education and a pathway to higher education, and for the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and humanitarian organizations to acknowledge their work and engage with them.

    A teacher at one of the schools mentioned, “We are spending money to ensure education quality, as if we were a government, but we are not a government, we are simply refugees.” Leaders and teachers offered to collaborate with UNICEF and humanitarian organizations on examinations, quality assurance, and improved teaching.

    Sources indicate that the vast majority of Rohingya students rely on donor-funded humanitarian education programs. Humanitarian groups providing education, coordinated by UNICEF, received just US$29 million from donors towards their 2025 budget request of $72 million, resulting in “learning centers” in the refugee camps closing for months. The education sector laid off teachers, cancelled an early education program, and cut teacher trainings and other programs. In October 2026, a humanitarian education official told Human Rights Watch: “We are struggling to maintain the most basic services. Even textbooks are [insufficient].… We cannot ensure children receive materials like a pencil, a notebook.... Learning centers were damaged by mudslides and climate events, but we do not have funding to carry out repairs.”.

    Several Rohingya instructors at learning centers that rely on humanitarian funds confirmed the lack of resources. A grade 1 instructor mentioned his classroom had no whiteboard, markers, desks, or benches, and students had to share textbooks, pens, and exercise books. A grade 3 instructor worried that “three students are using one set of textbooks.” Rather than teaching one class for the full school day, learning center instructors teach students in two “shifts” per day.

    Even after humanitarian agencies reduced their education funding request to $53 million for 2026, donors had pledged only $36 million by mid-October, leaving learning centers at risk of closing again, humanitarian officials remarked. The World Bank and Education Cannot Wait have provided or pledged funding, but this alone is insufficient. The United States had paid for half the Rohingya education budget before halting its funding in 2025. Globally, humanitarian education funding has fallen by 20 percent since 2023.

    Sources indicate that all states are obligated to provide children access to quality education without discrimination, regardless of their refugee status. The Inter-Agency Network for Education in Emergencies’ Minimum Standards emphasize the importance of community leadership and participation in the design and implementation of education programming.

    Recent findings suggest that “Rohingya children are eager to learn,” noted a Rohingya teacher in the camps. “The problem is that their education has been repeatedly interrupted by circumstances beyond their control. Education needs to be treated as a right, not a temporary humanitarian project.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I may not live in Ohio anymore, but there are some Ohio legal news stories I continue to follow. Here's one.

    Soon-to-be-former Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) sued his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno), for defamation. Now that suit has been dismissed, and arguably in the worst way for Miller: The court concluded that the core underlying allegation is "substantially true.".

    According to recent reports, miller filed the suit after the Daily Mail published a story reporting that Miller "hurled a pot of boiling water" at Moreno during an argument, and later wrote a note apologizing for the incident. As the court notes, an audio recording (that Miller released somehow thinking it would exonerate him) confirms the core of the claim. From the opinion:.

    It has been revealed that an audio recording of the parties discussing the incident supports Defendant Moreno's contention of truth. Defendant Moreno confronted Plaintiff about pouring "bowling hot water on me." Although Plaintiff denies pouring hot water on her neck, he further admits the incident occurred. Plaintiff specifically stated "it was never done to hurt you with intent." Plaintiffs intent is irrelevant to the basic fact of whether the incident occurred, which addresses the element of falsity.

    Plaintiff maintains that the gist or sting of hurling a pot of boiling water is "categorically different" than the actions Plaintiff states actually occurred. It is Plaintiffs burden to support his claims with credible, admissible evidence. Plaintiff has not shown that the statement about dousing Defendant Moreno with boiling hot water are false. The imputation that Plaintiff poured or doused Defendant Moreno with hot water is substantially true.

    The court also noted the lack of any evidence that Moreno was responsible for the Daily Mail's publication of the claims.

    The court dismissed Miller's suit with prejudice and awarded costs and attorney fees. Additional litigation arising out of the Miller-Moreno divorce is pending, and it's always possible Miller will appeal. Moreno is not the first woman to accuse Miller of abuse.

    More background from the Washington Post here.

    [Note: As initially posted, I referred to Miller as "Former Rep. Miller." OF course, he is not yet a former representative, as his term has not yet ended, so I have updated the post accordingly.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 12:42 pm CST.

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

    Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

    Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

    Industry observers note that “This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law said. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

    Sources indicate that A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

    Chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A United Nations budgetary advisory committee has proposed sweeping cuts to the Afghanistan accountability mechanism, established by consensus by the UN Human Rights Council in October 2025 following years of negotiations.

    The Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan was created to support efforts to hold the Taliban and others responsible for international crimes in Afghanistan to account. It is expected to include a focus on the Taliban’s crimes against humanity of gender persecution. Like similar mechanisms for Myanmar and Syria, it was designed to collect and preserve evidence and prepare files to support criminal prosecutions. Its formation followed years of campaigning by Afghan and international human rights groups on the basis that it could be a key tool in securing justice for victims of grave abuses. Its investigations could also act as a deterrent for current Taliban commanders.

    In a report prepared for the UN General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, which makes budget decisions, the Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ) recommended cutting 7 of 17 posts for 2027 with little explanation – including investigators, legal officers, security personnel, and administrative staff.

    According to recent reports, together with cuts made last year based on its recommendations, implementation of these recommendations would mean cutting by over a third the mechanism’s staffing for 2027, significantly hampering its ability to deliver on its mandate. The cuts would hit particularly hard given the original budget proposal was already scaled back by states negotiating its creation, mindful of the UN financial crisis, as compared to similar mechanisms for Syria and Myanmar.

    The budget advisory committee’s recommendation that the mechanism rely on other parts of the UN for communications, security and administrative support, rather than its own dedicated staff, also risks undermining its independence, a key feature of any criminal probe. The mechanism’s operational independence is intended to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of its work, and security of its staff, witnesses and victims. It is vital given the sensitive nature of its investigations and the risk of political interference.

    UN member states should reject these proposed cuts and approve the original modest budget requested by the secretary-general — something the General Assembly has done in the past. They should respect the Human Rights Council’s decision and ensure the mechanism can begin its investigations safely, securely and effectively—without further delays.

    ICC: Afghanistan Decision Risks Narrowing Access to Justice

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • The ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision.
    • According to recent reports, “Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (The Hague) – An International Criminal Court (ICC) decision risks hindering a path to justice for victims of grave crimes committed in Afghanistan, Human Rights Watch stated today. On November 12, 2026, an ICC pretrial chamber, citing a lack of activity, effectively closed the court’s situation dealing with crimes by US, Afghan government, and other forces prior to the Taliban’s August 2021 takeover.

    The ICC prosecutor’s office on November 13 sought to appeal the decision and to seek a stay of the closure decision. Research by Human Rights Watch and others over many years has documented war crimes and crimes against humanity by the Taliban; the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), an ISIS-affiliated group; Afghan government forces; and US military and Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) forces.

    According to recent reports, “Victims of serious international crimes committed by warring parties during Afghanistan’s long conflict have faced many roadblocks to justice,” noted Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “The ICC judges’ decision threatens to compound barriers to future accountability for US and Afghan government forces.”.

    In its initial 2017 request to open an investigation in Afghanistan, the prosecution cited alleged crimes by US military and CIA forces including torture and cruel treatment, outrages upon personal dignity, and rape and other forms of sexual violence “pursuant to a policy approved by the US authorities.” Regarding Afghan government forces, it cited alleged torture, sexual violence against detainees and civilians, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial executions.

    With respect to the Taliban’s forces, the crimes included directing attacks on the civilian population and other protected entities, murder, political and gender-based persecution, and the use of child soldiers. During the 20-year conflict, none of the warring parties demonstrated the will to meaningfully deliver justice for crimes committed by their personnel, Human Rights Watch said.

    In a recent development, in March 2020, ICC judges authorized the court’s prosecutor to investigate all alleged crimes falling within the ICC’s jurisdiction in Afghanistan, an ICC member country, since May 1, 2003. The prosecutor was also authorized to investigate crimes if sufficiently linked to the situation and the armed conflict that were committed in the territory of another ICC member country since July 1, 2002. The investigation was paused while the prosecution, and subsequently, the court’s judges considered a request by the then-Afghanistan government to defer ICC proceedings in favor of prosecutions the government asserted it was pursuing. The court’s judges concluded in 2022 that any cases pursued by the former government were at best a “very limited fraction” of those that would be covered by an ICC investigation.

    Since investigations resumed in 2022, the prosecution has indicated it would focus on alleged crimes by the Taliban and the ISKP, while deprioritizing alleged crimes by Afghan security forces and US personnel. In November 2024, in what is known as a state referral, six countries requested the ICC prosecutor to investigate “crimes committed against women and girls after the Taliban takeover in 2021” within the existing investigation. The investigations have yielded four arrest warrants against senior Taliban officials, including its supreme leader, for gender persecution, spotlighting the Taliban’s brutal repression of women, girls, gender non-conforming persons, and their allies.

    Victims and their families, along with Human Rights Watch and other nongovernmental organizations, have criticized the focus on Taliban abuses as creating a double standard, and have repeatedly urged the ICC prosecutor’s office to expand its investigations.

    Earlier in 2026, a pretrial chamber decision in related proceedings led to the separation of the court’s Afghanistan situation—open since 2020—into two different situations, one concerning abuses by Taliban forces since August 2021, and the other covering all other aspects of the originally authorized investigation. The prosecution has appealed in those related proceedings. Only the situation which concerns Taliban abuses, since August 2021, continues under the November 12 closure decision.

    The judges in the November 12 decision relied on a recently adopted court regulation permitting them to close out situation records if the prosecution has provided notice that it had “decide[d] not to initiate an investigation or determine[d] that he or she does not anticipate any further investigatory or prosecutorial activities” in that situation. The prosecution has recently asked the court to close the record in several situations in which it had decided not to initiate an investigation.

    In a recent development, however, the pretrial chamber in this ruling acted on its own initiative. During the proceedings that led to the separation of the Afghanistan situation into two, the prosecution indicated that it was pursuing three lines of inquiry; two concerning alleged Taliban crimes since August 2021, and one concerning alleged ISKP crimes since 2016. The chamber appears to have treated this indication as notification that the prosecution did not intend to pursue other aspects of the originally authorized investigation. It suggested in the closure decision that if the prosecution wished to pursue other lines of inquiry it could request authorization to do so in the future, a process that took more than two years to resolve when the prosecution first sought an Afghanistan investigation in 2017.

    Among other grounds in its appeal, the prosecution notes that it did not provide any notification under this regulation. In the related proceedings, the prosecution had indicated that it did not intend to provide any such notification.

    The court’s decision comes as the ICC faces increasing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick” if necessary to avoid any prosecution of Americans or Israelis. The Trump administration has imposed sanctions on the court that threaten its ability to operate, along with sanctions on several of its judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and a UN human rights expert. Human Rights Watch, together with three other organizations, is challenging the sanctions in US federal court.

    In a recent development, the judges also relied on their own observations that there are “significant limitations to the [p]rosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence,” and that the prosecution had yet to submit arrest warrant applications related to the ISKP. The ICC initially refused to authorize an Afghanistan investigation in 2019, in a decision Human Rights Watch described, at the time, as rewarding obstructionist behavior by states. That decision, overturned by the ICC appeals chamber, was handed down as the court faced hostility by the US government under the first Trump administration.

    “The ICC acts as a critical court of last resort when other avenues to justice are closed,” Evenson stated. “ICC member countries should do all they can to protect the ICC from US attempts to obstruct justice in the cases before it.”.

    • Recent findings suggest that the Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced Imran Aliyev, Meclis.info’s co-founder, to 10 years in prison, and Elgiz Gahraman, another co-founder and data analyst, to nine years.
    • Launched in 2023, Meclis.info published analyses of Azerbaijan's parliament, scrutinizing lawmakers’ attendance, voting records, and public statements.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that an Azerbaijani court sentenced two activists affiliated with Meclis.info, an independent platform monitoring the country’s parliament, to lengthy prison terms on dubious financial crime charges on November 12, 2026. These are the latest convictions as part of a wider crackdown that has seen scores of journalists, human rights defenders, and civic activists prosecuted on politically motivated charged since late 2023.

    Recent findings suggest that the Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced Imran Aliyev, Meclis.info’s co-founder, to 10 years in prison, and Elgiz Gahraman, another co-founder and data analyst, to nine years. A third defendant, the platform’s accountant Tamella Musayeva, received a suspended prison sentence. All three were convicted of illegal entrepreneurship, money laundering, currency smuggling, tax evasion, and document forgery.

    Launched in 2023, Meclis.info published analyses of Azerbaijan's parliament, scrutinizing lawmakers’ attendance, voting records, and public statements. Aliyev has been in detention since his arrest in April 2024. Gahraman and Musayeva were placed under police supervision in February 2025; Gahraman was taken into custody in the courtroom after the verdict.

    It has been revealed that during the trial, Aliyev acknowledged receiving foreign grants, but denied any criminal wrongdoing, maintaining that the prosecution was retaliation for Meclis.info’s work. His lawyer argued that failure to register grants constituted, at most, an administrative offense. Human Rights Watch has documented how Azerbaijani authorities use restrictive legislation and arbitrary registration practices to make it virtually impossible for independent groups to operate and receive foreign funding lawfully.

    Aliyev testified in April that police had beaten him, subjected him to electric shocks, and pressured him to sign documents without a lawyer present following his arrest. The Interior Ministry failed to effectively investigate the allegations.

    This is not Gahraman’s first politically motivated prosecution. Arrested on drug charges in 2016, he was sentenced to prison in 2017 and released by presidential pardon in March 2019. The European Court of Human Rights found in January that his earlier detention had been intended to punish him for his civic and political activism.

    Azerbaijani authorities should immediately release Aliyev, Gahraman, and all others imprisoned on politically motivated charges, overturn the unjust convictions, and end the misuse of foreign funding regulations to silence independent civic groups and media.
